Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 158 — Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 420, Thiru-nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-navukkarasu Swamigal and Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman arrive at the sthalam known as Vedaranyam, which is called Thiru-maraikkadu in Tamil.

Here, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings a pathikam and opens the sacred doors that were worshipped and sealed by the Vedas. Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman then sings a pathikam and causes the opened doors to be sealed again. Vedaranyam is the sthalam where this wondrous sacred history unfolded. Before contemplating this sacred history, let us briefly consider the sthala puranam (legend of the place) and special features of Vedaranyam. This Thiru-sthalam, Vedaranyam, is located on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is the one hundred and twenty-fifth sthalam.

This Thiru-sthalam is situated on the seashore. This Thiru-sthalam, Vedaranyam, possesses unique greatness due to its natural and man-made features, including the sea, sand dunes, forests, temples, and gopurams. One can reach this Thiru-sthalam from cities such as Mayuram, Kumbakonam, and Nagapattinam. The land is good, sandy soil. It is a sthalam surrounded on all four sides by screwpine hedges, water-thorn forests, small reservoirs, and salt marshes. This sthalam is located in the Neythal region, which is a coastal area.

In the Thiru-murais, it is referred to as Maraivanam, Maraikkadu, Vedavanam, and Vedaranyam. In the Puranas, it is called Vedavanam and Satyagiri. This sthalam also bears the sacred name Adisethu. It is commonly known as Vedaranyam. In inscriptions, this sthalam is referred to as Thiru-maraikkadu in Umbalanadu, Kunnoornadu. All these names are based on the history of the Vedas worshipping the Lord here.

Satyagiri means an imperishable mountain. This is the name of the sand hill at Kodiakkarai. History states that there was once a mountain here, from which a river called Satya Nadi originated and merged with the sea, and later merged with the Veda Nadi. It is called Adisethu because it was here that Adi Rama first built a bridge to go to Lanka. This sthalam is also known as Then Kailayam and Dakshina Kailasam. This Thiru-sthalam is one of the Sapta Vidanga sthalams.

Therefore, it is structured like the Thiru-varur Poongoyil. It has an east-facing sanctum. Inside the temple, there are two circumambulatory paths (prakarams), and adjacent to the temple wall is a matha complex, beyond which are streets for chariots on all four sides. The Rajagopuram (main tower) on the east has five tiers and nine kalasams (finials) at the top. Adjacent to the gopuram, in the southeast corner, is the Manikkarnikai Theertham (sacred pond) inside. There are the Navakannikai Mandapam, Viswamithra well, Madappalli (kitchen), and Nandavanam (flower garden).

On the upper side, there are Shiva Linga temples established and worshipped by the Pandiyas, the Melagopuram (upper tower), and adjacent to it, the Brahmagathi Medai and the shrines of Veeragathi Vinayagar and Melakumarar. On the north side, at the head of the prakaram, the Amman (Goddess) temple stands separately. Inside the Amman temple, in the prakaram, there are temples for Vinayagar in the Kanni Moolai and Kumarar in the Vayu Moolai. Temples are located. To the north of the Vedavaneswarar temple, there are the Kasi Viswanathar shrine, a sixteen-pillared mandapam, a swing mandapam, and yagasalas (sacrificial halls). In the inner prakaram, Sundarar, Pichadanar, and Ardhanareeswarar are enshrined respectively.

There are also the sixty-three Nayanmar idols and their processional idols, Kanni Vinayagar, Vedavana Pillaiyar, Murugan, Lakshmi, Saneesar, Saraswati, Annapoorani, Durga, and other shrines. This place is one of the Kozhili sthalams, so the Navagrahas (nine planets) are arranged in a row without being in retrograde motion. In the central mandapam, Tyagarajar, Vedaranyeswarar, and other deities are enshrined. Behind the Moolattanam (main sanctum) of Udayar, Uma Maheswar appears in a bridal form. Annually, on the Saptami day of the Purvapaksha in the month of Chithirai, sandalwood paste is applied to the bridal deity. It is applied.

The sthala Vinayagar here is Veeragathi Pillaiyar. He got this name because he removed the sin of Veeragathi that followed Rama. The Kshetra Kovai Pillai Tamil states this as “Veeragathi Theertharul seyyum Vinayagan, Thiru-maraikkattinil Ramar pinne thodarnthu varum.” He is located in the outer prakaram opposite the Melagopuram. In this Thiru-koyil, the Moolavar is Vedaranyeswarar, a Shiva Linga form.

The Lord has sacred names such as Vedanayagar, Vedavaneswarar, and Maraikkattisar. The Thiru-murais and Puranas have worshipped the Lord. Inscriptions refer to the Lord by the names Vedavanamudaiya Nayagar and Vedavanamudaiyar. Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman has sung, “Vedangal potri malaraal vazhipadu sey Ma Maraikkadar.” Behind Vedavaneswarar in the Moolasthanam, the enshrined Lord is Maraikkattu Uraiyum Manalar, the Lord who appeared in a bridal form as Ammaiyappar to Agastya. Appar Swamigal has sung, “Malaiyartham magalodum Madhevan serum Maraikkadu.” The sacred name of the Goddess in this sthalam is Veenavatha Vidushini. This is a Sanskrit name.

In Tamil, the Thiru-murais refer to the Mother’s sacred name as “Yaazhai pazhitha mozhi Umaiyal.” Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has sung, “Yaazhai pazhithathanna mozhi mangaiyodu pangan.” Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman has sung about the Mother as “Pannin ner mozhiyal.” Next, the Tyagarajar here is one of the Tyagamurthis bestowed by Indra to Musukunda Chakravarthi. The dance he performs here is called Hamsa Natanam. Hamsa Natanam means a dance where one moves slowly, taking steps like a swan. It is a dance that moves slowly, taking steps like a swan. Next is Bhuvani Vidangar, an emerald Shiva Linga form enshrined in a casket within the Tyagaraja shrine. This deity is bathed twice daily.

This idol is made of green gemstone. Next is Durga, a highly worshipped deity here. She is enshrined in the first prakaram of the Lord’s temple, facing south on the north side. Durga serves as the family deity for many. Next is the Nataraja idol in the Thiru-koyil. The Vedaranyam Sthala Puranam states that this deity is one of the eighteen dances.

Next is Kaatchi Koduthavar (the one who gave darshan). This is a processional idol. This deity is named Rishabantaka Murthi, one of the twenty-five Maheswara forms. One cannot help but be captivated by the beauty of this form, with a smile, the right hand resting on the head of the bull, and the left hand on the thigh. No one’s heart can remain untouched by the beauty upon seeing this form. The next deity is Chandrasekhara Murthi.

This is also a Utsava Thiru-meni (processional idol). During festivals, on days when Tyagesar does not go out, it is customary to crown this deity. This is known as Chandrasekhara Pattabhishekam.

Now, regarding the Theerthams (sacred waters) in this sthalam, there are ninety-six Theerthams here. There are Theerthams such as Manikkarnikai, Viswamithra Theertham, Vedamrita Theertham, Vedanadi, and Kotti Theertham. It is an ancient tradition to divide these ninety-six Theerthams into six pilgrimages and bathe in them. These six pilgrimages are Vishnu Yatra, Sethu Yatra, Dakshinamana Brahma Yatra, and Uttaramana. The methods of bathing in these are described in the Sthala Puranam. Vedaranyam is a Thiru-sthalam that is special in all three aspects: Murthi (deity), Sthalam (place), and Theertham (sacred water).

This Thiru-sthalam, Vedaranyam, was worshipped by the Vedas. It removed the Veeragathi (sin of killing a warrior) from Rama. It showed the bridal form to Agastya. It made a rat that kindled a lamp into a Mahabali (great sacrifice). It was worshipped by Musukunda Chakravarthi. It is praised by the proverb “Vedaranyam vilakku azhagu” (The lamp of Vedaranyam is beautiful).

It was worshipped by Nachikethas, Ketu, Gautama, Manu, Mandhata, Dasaratha, Viswamithra, Vasishta, and others. It was praised and glorified by the Thiru-murai scholars and other poets. The sacred doors, which were closed by the Vedas, were opened and closed by Thiru-navukkarasu Swamigal and Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman here, a glory sung about. The sculptural excellence of the Vedaranyam temple, with its rich corbels, potikas, yalis, stone chains hanging from the mouths of yalis, The stone balls rolling in the mouths of the yalis, and the creeper carvings on the pillars, are all exceptionally fine and beautiful. On the ceiling slab of the front mandapam of the sanctum, the twelve zodiac signs are carved. The twenty-seven constellations are arranged according to their respective Dhyana Slokas.

The bridal form of the Lord, enshrined behind the Moolattanam, is exceedingly beautiful. All the Utsava Murthis (processional deities) of this Thiru-sthalam are very ancient and beautiful.

Now, regarding the Sthala Vriksha (sacred tree) here, the Vanni tree in front of the Lord’s temple is the Sthala Vriksha. Mostly, Sthala Vrikshas are associated with historical events. In that sense, originally, the Sthala Vriksha was a dense forest.

In this context, the Vanni tree here is the place where Agastya performed penance, desiring to see the bridal form, and attained Siddhi (spiritual perfection).

Therefore, it has a connection to Puranic history. The Punnai tree opposite the Amman shrine is also considered a Sthala Vriksha. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar sings in his Thiru-kurunthogai, “Surakkum punnaigal soozh Maraikkadaro.” In both prakarams, there are mandapams such as the Rajanarayana Mandapam, Sixteen-Pillared Mandapam, Vanniyadi Mandapam, Chettiyar Mandapam, Purana Mandapam, Mahamandapam, and Ardha Mandapam. Around Manikkarnikai, there are tiled mandapams suitable for performing Shiva Puja and Japa. There are also the Vasanta Mandapam and Sethupathi Mandapam. The hall where Nataraja Peruman is enshrined is in the inner prakaram.

This is also known as Devar Thozhu Mandram and Devabhakta Sabai.

Now, let us briefly contemplate the Puranic history of the Vedaranyam sthalam. Thirumal, incarnated as Adi Rama, intended to go to Lanka and destroy Ravana. He investigated which place would be easy to cross the sea. He concluded that Vedaranyam was the best place and arrived here. With the help of the Vanara warriors who accompanied him, he built a bridge. He went to Lanka, killed Ravana, rescued Sita Piratti, and returned to Ayodhya.

On his way back over the bridge, the sin of Brahmagathi (killing a Brahmin), incurred by killing Ravana, afflicted Rama as a Brahma Rakshasa. Due to this, Rama became disheartened. The sages witnessed this state. The sages requested Rama, saying that if he meditated on Shiva Peruman by chanting the Sri Panchaksharam at the very place where he built the bridge, this sin would be removed. Rama Peruman, following the advice of the sages, broke the bridge in three places with his bow, turning it into a sea. He then sought to know which place was suitable for performing penance with sixty-eight thousand sages to attain Siddhi.

At that time, Jabali Muni, the chief of the sages, addressed Rama Peruman, saying, “To the north of this Sethu, there is a mountain called Satyagiri. A river called Satya Nadi flows there. During the time you built the Sethu Bandhanam, that river merged with the sea. That river is now flowing northwards into the sea as Uttarakami. If you bathe there and perform penance on that mountain, the Lord will appear, grant your wishes, and remove this blemish.” Rama Peruman, following the sage’s words, performed penance. Shiva Peruman, pleased with his penance, appeared in the form of a Shiva Lingam with the Manikkarnikai Theertham at noon on a auspicious day in the month of Panguni, when it was a full moon and Uttara Nakshatra.

Along with that, he appeared as a luminous form, bearing a snake and the Ganga river on his sacred head, shining like a thousand suns, holding a deer and a battle-axe, adorned with a Kondrai garland, He revealed his complete sacred form. Rama Peruman, seeing the sacred form of Shiva Peruman, worshipped him with tears of joy in his eyes. Shiva Peruman addressed Rama, saying, “Rama, the sins like Brahmagathi that you committed have been removed. We have come here with the Manikkarnikai Theertham to remove your blemish. All the sins of those who bathe in it will be removed.” In response to Rama Peruman’s request, Shiva Peruman continues to bless devotees even today as a Shiva Linga form, facing east, to the west of the Veda Nadi.

Thus, this sthalam became known as Adi Sethu, worshipped by Adi Rama. It is imperishable even during the Brahma Yuga. The sound world of Vedas and Agamas, and the material universes, both animate and inanimate, merge into it. When the world is recreated, Shiva Peruman will emerge from this Linga form and instruct Brahma on the principles of Vedas and Agamas. Just like the Manikkarnika Ghat in Kasi, the Theertham blessed by the Lord in Thiru-maraikkadu is Manikkarnikai. This pond, like the Lord’s right eye, shines along the outer wall.

Since Shiva Peruman appeared here at noon for Rama Peruman, bathing in this pond at noon is considered special. Bathing in Kasi Manikkarnikai in the morning and in this sthalam’s Manikkarnikai at noon yields equal Shiva Punya (merit). Shiva Peruman blessed the Vedas, the six Angas, Agamas, and Puranas so that all people might live disciplined and within bounds. The great Brahmins, free from faults like the desire to hoard wealth for the next day, would recite these Vedas and, by living according to their teachings, served as guides for others. As time passed, those Brahmins deviated from their observances and They attempted to recite the Vedas for their livelihood. As a result, the Vedic mantras lost their power.

Realizing this, the four Vedas took human form and worshipped the Lord, desiring to regain their lost power. They reached this sthalam, Vedaranyam, which had the ancient name Satyagiri. They began to worship Sambhu, who resides in Satyagiri. To the north of Vedanathan, at a distance of a hundred bow-lengths, they created a large lake named Vedamritham after themselves. Daily, they bathed in it, immersed themselves in Manikkarnikai, and during the times suitable for bathing in the sea, they immersed themselves in the Satya Nadi, which is the sea, and worshipped Shiva Peruman without deviating from the Sivagama path. Shiva Peruman, pleased by the worship of the four Vedas, appeared as Vedavana Peruman in a Shiva Linga form at dawn during the auspicious Vyatipata Punyakalam in the month of Margazhi.

He appeared in form and addressed the Vedas, saying, “Vedas, you have worshipped me with sincere devotion for many years.

“Therefore, I am pleased. I have come here to grant all the desired boons to anyone who worships me as you have. Ask for the boons you wish.” The Vedas, addressing Shiva Peruman, said, “Oh Lord of Grace, who is moved by love, we have no shortcomings by your divine grace.

“However, Lord, we wish to ask for some boons according to your will. We have a desire: we wish to remain here forever, worshipping you like this. Even if many Brahma Kalpas pass, we wish to live in this sthalam, taking all births as grass, shrubs, and trees. Whatever birth we take, our duty should be to behold, worship, and praise you.

“Therefore, this sthalam Should be known by our names as Vedavanam, Vedaranyam, and Maraikkadu. The river here should be called Veda Nadi, the pond Vedamritham, the Lord Vedaranyeswar, and the Mother Vedanayaki.” Thus, they requested that everything in this sthalam should have the prefix “Veda.” They also requested, “Annually, whoever bathes in Vedamritham and Veda Nadi during this Mahavyapata Yoga and beholds you, should attain worldly happiness and liberation in the afterlife. Please grant such boons.” Shiva Peruman, considering the selfless and generous nature of the Veda Purushas, said to the Vedas, “We appreciate your quality of wishing for the well-being of all, with the underlying desire that your name should spread everywhere. You We have granted the boons you requested. May you, who are virtuous, from a good lineage, and unwavering in your observances, always live with the abundant power of mantras in the mouths of Brahmins. Whoever recites you, the Vedas, along with your Angas, will also attain the positions granted by us.” Thus, Shiva Peruman spoke and then merged into the Shiva Lingam.

“The Satya Nadi, which originated from the Satyagiri mountain at Kodiakkarai, merges with the Veda Nadi, which is the sea of the sanctum, for a distance of ten yojanas. Those who remember, touch, or bathe in that river become Jeevan Muktas (liberated while living). Those who bathe in the Veda Nadi and worship Vedavaneswarar will attain long life, Shiva Gnanam (divine knowledge), and all desired objects. If the Vedas themselves bathe in this river, it means that sacred rivers like the Ganga also bathe to cleanse their sins. The meaning of this is that since Kodi Theertham is the southeastern corner of the ocean, and because the tip of the bow of the primordial Rama was immersed in it, and because it removes countless sins of devotees who bathe in it, granting them countless blessings, it is named Kodi Theertham. Those who immerse themselves in this Theertham at any time will attain liberation.

“However, it is most excellent to bathe during the auspicious periods of Vyathipatha Yoga, Dakshinayana, Uttarayana, the beginning of the month, Amavasya, Pournami, and Vishu. At this Thalam, on a Sunday, during the seventh Thithi of the waxing moon in the month of Chithirai, at noon, Lord Shiva revealed to Sage Agathiyar, who had come south, the wedding form of Lord Shiva and Parvathi that took place in Kailash. Another important historical event took place at the Thiru-Vedaranyam temple, the Thiru-Vedavaneswarar temple.

“One day, the lamp burning in the sanctum sanctorum where the Lord resides dimmed slightly. Lord Shiva, addressing Uma Devi, said, “Whoever rekindles this lamp, we will grant them kingship in this world and Shiva-gathi in the next.” Uma Devi smiled and submitted, “The Ardha Jama puja is over, and the doors are closed.

“After this, when the Devas are in solitude, who will come inside and rekindle the lamp? The boon you speak of is wondrous.” The Lord said, “Wait and see.” At that moment, a mouse climbed onto the lamp to drink the ghee in it. As it did, the lamp was rekindled and burned brightly with clear light.

“Lord Shiva blessed that mouse to attain kingship, filled with all riches. That mouse was born as the son of a king named Virochana, and ruled the three worlds under the name Mahabali. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has sung this history in his Thiru-Pathigam.

“Moreover, this history is also found in the Sthala Puranam. Emperor Mahabali, by the merit of having rekindled the lamp as a mouse, became a king.

“Therefore, kings have had faith and conviction in lighting lamps.

“Thus, inscriptions show that most kings donated gold, land, and cattle for the lamps of Thiru-Vedaranyam.

“Therefore, the proverb “Vedaranyam lamp is beautiful” also originated from this. All these are facts and Puranic histories about this sacred place called Thiru-Vedaranyam. To this glorious Thalam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arrive. The Vedas worshipped Thiru- The miraculous act of these two great personages singing Pathigams to open the closed doors and then to close them again is about to take place here. Let us contemplate on that.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 159 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 421. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arrive at the sacred Thiru-Marai-Kadu, known as Vedaranyam. Vedaranyam is a coastal Thalam belonging to the Neythal Thinai.

Therefore, the land and primary elements appropriate to that Thinai flourish there. Punnai trees and pearls brought by the sea are the primary elements of the Neythal Thinai.

Additionally, there are salt pans in Vedaranyam that produce salt. There are groves where fragrant Punnai flowers bloom. Salt, which adds taste to food, is produced there.

Thus, providing sweetness to the mind and body, guiding people’s minds towards the path of liberation and helping them, Such an environment exists in Thiru-Marai-Kadu. Here arrive the Lord of Southern Pukali and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal. This Thalam is close to the sea and its sandy shores. The Vedas worshipped Lord Shiva, who resides in this Thalam as a Brahmin.

Lord Shiva is a Brahmin, so the Vedas worshipped Him. The worship by the Vedas means that the presiding deities of the Vedic mantras took form and worshipped the Shiva Lingam.

In this way, the Vedas worshipped the Lord and then closed the doors. Closing the doors with appropriate rituals, actions, and mantras after opening them for worship and before the next worship is the meaning of “Thiru-Kaappu Seythal.” The meaning of “Thiru-Kaappu Seythal” is to close and lock the doors with appropriate rituals, actions, and mantras after opening them for worship and before the next worship. The Vedas once worshipped the Shiva Lingam here and then departed.

From that day until now, when the Nayanmars arrived, those doors have remained closed. It is a rule of Shiva temple darshan that those who go to the temple should worship the temple entrances and the temple tower before entering. According to this, both Nayanmars worship the sacred entrance of this temple. This ancient sacred entrance, closed by the Vedas, remains locked. No devotees capable of opening these locked doors have come yet, so it remains locked.

Therefore, everyone goes through another entrance next to that entrance and worship Lord Shiva. These entrances are locked with mantra-bound latches.

Therefore, no one with the spiritual power to recite similar mantras and perform actions to undo the mantra-power of the Vedas has come here yet.

Thus, those entrances remain closed.

Therefore, Shiva devotees and people go through another adjacent entrance to perform worship. The point here is that a door closed by the Vedas can only be opened by something similar.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman sing the Thevara Thiru-Pathigams, which are Tamil Vedas, to open the closed door and then again to lock that door. This is about to happen now. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman hear from the devotees there about the closed temple doors and their history. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having heard this history and background information, addresses Appar Swamigal, saying, “Appare, please sing so that the sacred doors in front of the temple, which the exalted Vedas worshipped, may open, allowing us both to enter and worship the Lord, the God of Gods, without hindrance.” Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman thus speaks to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Having understood the situation, the Lord of Thoni-Puram, who is the ocean, “Appar, sing so that the sacred doors in front, which the exalted Vedas worshipped, may open, allowing us to enter and worship the Lord without hindrance.” Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasar, in his profound nature, was addressed by Pillaiyar.

Therefore, he began to sing, taking the words “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal.” As a result, the sacred doors, which were closed, opened. The Lord, who wears the southern cool garland, removed the sacred lock. The Thiru-Kadaikkappu was sung, “Enneer Irakkamonrilir.” As he sang and worshipped, by the grace of the true essence of Vedavanam, the jeweled doors, which were locked, opened in front of the loving devotees.

The Lord of the arts, along with the sage of wisdom, bowed down. The sound of the ocean and the roar of the Devas, along with the sound of the Vedas, resounded. Sekkizhar Peruman now describes the events that transpired in these three verses. The main direct doors of the temple are locked.

Therefore, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman asks Appar Swamigal, “Appare, please sing so that these doors may open.” All the people worship the Lord by going through the adjacent entrance, not through the main direct entrance. But Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman asks, “You and I must go through this main direct entrance to worship the Lord.

“Therefore, please sing so that the door may open.” He addresses him as “Appare.” When Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman first met Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in Sirkazhi, he addressed him as “Appare.” He uses the same address here to make this request. The implication here is that since he is Appar, he should be the one to sing to open the door. While Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman was present, Appar Swamigal did not initially intend to sing a Pathigam.

“Therefore, knowing this intention of Appar Swamigal, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman thus addressed Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who is Aludaiya Pillaiyar, spoke thus out of love.

“Therefore, as Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman requested, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal began a Thevara Thiru-Pathigam with the words “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal.” “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal” are the opening lines of the Thiru-Pathigam composed by Appar Swamigal for the opening of the temple doors. “Pan” refers to a musical arrangement that is unique to Tamil and naturally aligns with the vocal sound of women.

“Therefore, “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal” is the meaning expounded by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for the Ambika residing in Thiru-Marai-Kadu, Vedaranyam. We know that the sacred name of the Ambika here is Veena Vatha Vithushini. In Tamil, this is referred to as “Yazhai Pazhitha Mozhiyal.” Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman also sang in his Thiru-Pathigam, “Yazhai Pazhithanna Mozhi Mangai Oru Pangan.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings this very name as “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal.” The name “Yazhai Pazhitha Mozhi Ammai” has a negative connotation. If “Yazhai Pazhitha Mozhi” means that which surpasses the Yazh, then the question arises, what does it equal? It equals “Pan.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman explains it in an affirmative way as “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal,” meaning that which is equal to “Pan.” Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman begins his Thiru-Pathigam with “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal Umaipangaro” and composes it for the opening of the closed sacred doors. At the end of this, in the Thiru-Kadaikkappu, he sings, “Enneer Irakkamonrilir.” This Thiru-Pathigam consists of eleven verses.

“In ten of these verses, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman makes a plea to the Lord to open the door. “Kanni-nal umai kaana kathavinai thinnamaaga thirantharul seymine.” “Remove the strength of the long, great door; open the door. Open the great heavenly door; remove the distant door’s support. Open the door to be seen. Remove the affliction of the great door; remove the strength of the door; open the door.

“Open it firmly.” Thus, in ten verses, he pleads, “Open the door, O Lord!” In the eleventh verse, he pleads, “You have no compassion, O my Lord!” This Pathigam, sung with the plea to open the door, is the tenth Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thiru-Murai. Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam.

““Pannin Ner Mozhiyal Umaipangaro, Manninar” “O Lord, who resides in the sacred forest worshipped by those who endure! Open the door firmly so that we may see You with our eyes. O Lord, who resides in the red matted locks! O Lord, who is like the dark clouds!

“You who have taken us into Your fold, grant Your grace. Remove the strength of the long, great door. O Appar, who is the eight-formed one! O Lord, who burned the great city with a touch! O Lord, who wears the crown,” “O supreme Lord, who wears the crown!

“Open this door firmly. O Lord, who recited the rare four Vedas! O Lord, who burned the great city with a touch! O Lord, who wears the spreading loincloth! Open the great heavenly door. O Lord, who resides in the sacred forest on the mountain!

“O Lord, whose feet are worshipped by the arts! O Lord, whose form is like a priceless great gem! Remove the support of the distant door.” “O Lord, who resides in the sacred forest surrounded by blooming Thazhai and fragrant Arugam grass! O Lord, who is difficult for anyone to see! O Lord, open the door so that we may see You.

“O Lord, who smears the sacred white ash! O Lord, who resides in the endless, beautiful sacred forest! O Lord, remove the affliction of this great door so that Your devotees may come and worship You. O Lord, who wears the Ganga and resides in the beautiful sacred forest! O Lord, who shares half with the Mother,” “O Lord, who rides the bull!

“O my Lord, remove the strength of this incomparable door. O Lord, who smears the white ash! O Lord, who is the supreme one, who knows the beauty of the Pan! O Lord, who is the primordial one, who resides in the beautiful sacred forest! Open the firm door. O Lord, whom the celestials desire to meet!

“O Lord, whom the earthly beings worship, who resides in the sacred forest! Open the door firmly so that we may see You with our eyes.” “You who crushed the Rakshasa with your finger, you have no compassion, O my Lord! O Lord, who resides in the sacred forest surrounded by abundant Punnai trees! Open the door quickly.” 

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal sings this Thiru-Pathigam. “Pannin Ner Mozhiyal Pangare,” meaning, “O Lord, who shares half with the one whose language is like the Pan! Remove the great affliction of this door and open it so that we may see You directly with our eyes and so that devotees may come and worship You.” With this sentiment, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal sings this Thiru-Pathigam. “Pannin” Sekkizhar Peruman states that because Lord Shiva, who shares half with the one whose language is like the Pan, enjoyed the benefit of this, He delayed opening the door. Even though we perceive the Lord with our inner eye, he pleads that we should also see the Lord directly with our outer eyes through this entrance.

“These doors are very firmly and strongly locked because the Vedas came here, worshipped, and then closed these doors.

“Therefore, these are doors protected by mantras. That is why Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, throughout this Pathigam, sings about the strength of the door and the strength of its closure, referring to it as “Ma Kathavu,” “Periya Vaan Kathavam,” “Tholaivilaa Kathavam,” “Ma Kathavam,” “Maarilaa Kathavam,” and “Vali.” In the third verse, the word “Suvandar” appears, meaning one who possesses special marks. “Suvandu” means a mark or sign. “Suvadu” might have become “Suvandu.” The crescent moon, Ganga, and Nagasiram on the Lord’s head illustrate His supreme nature. This door is the direct path.

“Its closure has caused sorrow in the hearts of devotees.

“Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings, “Open this door to relieve that sorrow.” Thus, in ten verses, he sings to open the door. In the eleventh verse, he sings, addressing the Lord, “You have no compassion.” Even after Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman pleaded in ten verses for the door to open, the Lord did not grant His grace.

“Therefore, he sings, “You have no compassion,” in the eleventh verse. As soon as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sang thus, the sacred doors, which had been locked by the Vedas, opened. By the divine grace of the Lord, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and other devotees, as these doors opened, entered directly and worshipped the Lord. Their hair stood on end; they danced in ecstasy. Tears of joy flowed as they contemplated the Lord’s divine grace.

“Here, the Vedas of the Lord had locked the door, and the Thiru-Pathigam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the Tamil Veda, caused it to open.

“The Lord demonstrated this divine grace here so that everyone might realize that the Sanskrit Veda and the Tamil Veda proclaim the same ultimate truth. By the divine grace of the Lord, the true essence shining in Vedaranyam, the luminous jeweled door was opened, and the loving devotees, along with Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, entered through this opened entrance, praised and worshipped the Lord, prostrated themselves, bowed down, and rose. The shouts of the Devas and the sound of the Vedas resounded more loudly than the roar of the ocean. The assembly of devotees experienced great joy. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the sovereign of the devotees, and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the child-saint, immersed themselves in joy, entered, bowed down to the Lord, praised Him, sang Thiru-Pathigams, and with their bones melting and hearts overflowing, they worshipped the Lord.

“At this time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman Many Tamil garlands of hymns are sung.

“At this time, it is most appropriate, as Sivakavimani Aiyya writes, that the Thiru-Kurunthokai hymn, “Othamaal Kadal,” composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, should have been revealed before the Lord. This sacred hymn is the ninth Thiru-Pathikam of the fifth Thiru-Murai, a Thiru-Kurunthokai Thiru-Pathikam.

“Othamaal Kadal. The world is filled with women who worship the Lord of Marai-Kadu, who is loved and desired. By praising His feet, sins will vanish.

“The Lord of Marai-Kadu, who is difficult for all to see, looks upon His devotees. If we do not perform His service, we will not see Him.

“The Lord of Marai-Kadu, whose feet are worshipped by those who live in the world, has a beautiful form.

“The Lord of Marai-Kadu, who has a beautiful form, has a beautiful form. He is the wealth that delights in a small form, with a part of the body as a woman. He wears eight great flowers and has a round, matted, reddish-brown hair. He is the Lord of Marai-Kadu. He dances and sings the four Vedas. This is the place where He is lovingly present.

“The Lord of Marai-Kadu, surrounded by fields full of water lilies and lotuses, is the one who has taken a woman as a part of His body. He keeps a young white crescent moon and a snake in His matted hair. Those who praise Him without sleep even in their sleep are the Lord of Marai-Kadu, who has a beautiful form. The soft-footed maiden brought a tiger, and the five-headed serpent stood in fear.

“The Lord of Marai-Kadu, who is adorned with wealth and festivities, has taken Uma, the beautiful maiden, as a part of His body. He has placed the Ganga on His head.

“The Lord of Marai-Kadu, where conches wash up on the shore, keeps fire in His hand, not just the Ganga in His red matted hair. How beautiful it is! The ninth verse of this hymn is not available to us.

“Now, the tenth verse: The chariot of the one who showed no fault, the great mountain, the one who took the ten heads, the one who showed no fault, the one who made the Lord speak out, the one who showed no fault, our Lord, to praise you.

“Let us go on contemplating.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 160 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 422. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings a Thiru-Pathikam. The sacred door, which was locked by the Vedas, opens by the grace of the Lord.

Through that open door, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and other devotees enter the temple and worship the Lord. After worshipping, they come out through the same door. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, and other devotees come out of the temple. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman says to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the Kaundinya of Pukali, who partook of the nectar of wisdom that flowed from the breast of the mountain goddess, “Please sing so that the open door may close again.”

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman says to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Because, just as the previously closed doors remained closed, now the open doors should not remain open.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman tells Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Please sing so that the open doors may close again.” The power of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred wisdom, the sacred words of the Lord, is such that just as the Vedas locked the door, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words also have the power to lock the doors. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman tells Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Just as you asked me to sing to open the door, now I ask you...” I request you to sing again so that these doors may close. Because the doors that were closed have now opened. If the opened doors are closed again, then these doors can be opened and closed for worship continuously. That is why the Peruman makes this request.

In response to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s request, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the Lord of Sirkazhi and the Tamil poet, hearing Thiru-Navukkarasu’s polite words, begins to sing a Thiru-Pathikam. As soon as Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman began to sing the Thiru-Kadavu, the doors of the sacred temple closed with the very first verse. The doors closed with the very first song. By the grace of Shiva Peruman, who has a beautiful forehead with eyes. By the grace of Shiva Peruman, as soon as Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman began to sing, the sacred doors closed again with the very first song. They were locked.

Earlier, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had requested in ten songs that the door be opened. But when the Peruman delayed, he pleaded with great sorrow in the eleventh song, “You are without mercy,” and then the door opened.

But now, with the very first song sung by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the sacred doors closed.

Thus, the Lord bestowed His grace upon both Nayanmars in different ways.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman describes the Lord who bestowed such grace as having beautiful eyes that are responsible. “The ornament of the eye is compassion,” says the Thiru-Kural.

But here, Shiva Peruman bestows grace in different ways upon the two Nayanmars. When Shiva Peruman, who has a beautiful forehead adorned with compassionate eyes, is present, why does Sekkizhar Peruman sing about Him in this way? It is to illustrate that the greatness of the Lord’s compassionate gaze lies in His ability to bestow grace according to each individual’s capacity.

Similarly, in Thiru-Vizhimizhalai, the Lord’s grace provided coins with interest to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, but to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, He provided coins without interest, as we saw there in Thiru-Vizhimizhalai.

Now, the Thiru-Pathikam that begins with “Ippozhuthu Paadiya Thiru-Pathikam Enbadhu” (This Thiru-Pathikam that was sung now) is about the sacred doors that were previously locked by the Vedas.

Therefore, to lock those sacred doors again, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman begins this Thiru-Pathikam by starting with “Chathuram Marai Than” (The four Vedas) and then with “Marai” (Vedas).

Thus, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman begins this Thiru-Pathikam by placing the Vedas first. By the grace of the Lord, the doors closed with the very first verse. Seeing this, Aludaiya Pillaiyar and Aludaiya Arasu rejoiced, saying, “We have received this grace from our Lord,” and worshipped Him there. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman also completed the Thiru-Pathikam he had begun, sang it, and worshipped.

Thus, seeing these gracious acts performed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, where doors locked by the Vedas opened and then opened doors closed again, all the devotees were amazed. Their hair stood on end, tears of love flowed from their eyes, and they worshipped the feet of these two great ones, who were incomparable in every way.

Then, Sirkazhi Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal went to the sacred monastery. We saw earlier that in Thiru-Vizhimizhalai, both great ones stayed in separate monasteries.

But here, in Vedaranyam, we learn that both great ones are staying in the same sacred monastery. After reaching the sacred monastery, a worry comes to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s mind. He had sung ten songs, requesting the Lord to open the door, and then in the eleventh song, he sang, “You are without mercy.” After that, the Lord delayed and then opened the sacred door.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is now worried because the Lord opened the door after a long delay.

Therefore, opening the door was not Shiva Peruman’s sacred will. It seems that we have strongly urged the Lord by singing. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman thinks that he has achieved the act of opening the door by singing eleven songs and even forcefully saying to the Lord, “You are without mercy.” The Nayanar considers the act of closing the door with the very first song sung by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman to be easy.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman thinks, “I was unaware of the Lord’s sacred will.” “Ayarthal” means to desire. He worries, “It seems that opening the door was not Shiva Peruman’s sacred will. Without realizing this, I requested and desired to open the door.” The Lord’s sacred will, when desired, is easily achieved. What the Lord does not will, It is achieved only with great difficulty and effort.

Therefore, this desire to open the door was achieved after much fervent prayer and many efforts.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman grieves, thinking that this act was not in accordance with the Lord’s sacred will.

Furthermore, he thinks, “When there was no intention in the Lord’s sacred will to open the door, I dared to do it.” And he thinks, “The Lord is greatly compassionate, the embodiment of grace, and does nothing but grace. How could I have forcefully reproached such a Lord, saying, ‘You are without mercy,’ in the Thiru-Pathikam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman?” Therefore, he worries, considering this to be a mistake he made.

Moreover, he thinks, “We sang, ‘You are without mercy,’ to the Lord, who is the embodiment of compassion and does nothing but grace.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman fears that this has resulted in an offense against the Lord.

Thus, because he has offended the Lord, he feels that he is not fit to be with other devotees and should not join them. He worries that he does not have the qualification to be with other devotees because he has offended the Lord, and he withdraws to a corner of the sacred monastery. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman closes his eyes with worry, but he is not sleeping. He is not sleeping, but only closing his eyes, remaining in a state of alertness.

Thus, grieving, he keeps the sacred feet of Shiva Peruman, the Lord of Thiru-Marai-Kadu, in his mind and meditates on them without his thoughts wavering, and he closes his eyes. He falls into a state of conscious sleep, which is called ‘arithuyil’. While Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is in this state of conscious sleep, Shiva Peruman appears before him with a golden sacred body, adorned with sacred ashes, and blesses Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, saying, “We will be in Thiru-Vaimoor. Will you follow?” Shiva Peruman blesses him, saying, “We will be in Thiru-Vaimoor. Come and follow us there.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman comes out of the state of conscious sleep into a state of alertness. He composes the Thiru-Kurunthokai Thiru-Pathikam with the idea that the Lord went away after telling him to come there.

The Lord, having said, “I am in Thiru-Vaimoor, follow me,” has gone. This is the Lord’s command.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, determined to follow that command, rises and quickly departs from Thiru-Marai-Kadu. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the primordial Lord, goes before Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in the same form He had shown before. It is now a state of full consciousness for Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, free from dreams. The Lord, with the same form he saw in his dream, goes ahead, saying, “Follow me.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman now sees the Lord and follows Him. Sekkizhar Peruman says that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sang the Thiru-Kurunthokai Thiru-Pathikam with the idea, “He went there telling me to come, what is that?” That Thiru-Pathikam is the Thiru-Pathikam belonging to the sacred place of Thiru-Vaimoor, the fiftieth Thiru-Pathikam in the fifth Thiru-Murai, a Thiru-Kurunthokai Thiru-Pathikam.

“Where did He go, searching for me, and there He revealed Himself.

“The Lord of Thiru-Vaimoor, who appears in the south, went away saying, ‘Come there,’ what is that?” “The Lord of Marai-Kadu, who is worshipped by the earth, when I was thinking and thinking and sleeping, the Lord of Thiru-Vaimoor said, ‘I am the Lord,’ and went away saying, ‘Come to me,’ what is that?” “I saw Him in Thanjai, I said, ‘You are not proud.’ He said, ‘Do not fear, I have come to call you.’” I rejoiced and rose, and came running.

“The Lord of Vaimoor is indeed powerful. I did not see Him in a dream, I saw Him before my eyes. I did not go away, I came along with Him. I did not see Him on the way, what is it that I am caught in the whirlpool of the Lord of Vaimoor? “These are the bright ones, there is no other,” I thought and thought and rejoiced. “These are the clear ones, like Thiru-Vaimoor.

“Like the cunning ones, what did they do to me?” “If you are not in me, then you are of immeasurable greatness.

“The Lord of Vaimoor, who is the great God, is it false that He entered?” “The old coin, the reward obtained by singing, like those who remove sorrow and weariness, searching for me, saying, ‘Come to Thiru-Vaimoor,’ what is it that He has left me here?” He who sang to open, and then closed by singing a more refined Tamil verse, is He not the Lord of Thiru-Vaimoor, whose red matted hair bears the crescent moon? He is mad. Even if I pray to avoid what is not suitable for me, I thought, “He is the pure one who performs false grace.” “He came to me, saying, ‘Come to Thiru-Vaimoor,’ is it false that He entered the golden temple again?” “With one sacred foot, which is difficult to touch, He kicked the Rakshasa to return. I prayed to the light of Thiru-Vaimoor. When I said, ‘I will light it,’ He appeared.” 

“Thus, the Lord, in the same form He appeared in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s dream, went ahead, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman followed the Lord from Thiru-Marai-Kadu. Even though he received the nectar of boundless love in his hand, it was like not being able to eat it in his mouth.

“The Lord with the Ganga-laden matted hair went ahead, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman followed Him for a long distance. The great Shiva Peruman went ahead, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman tried to go near Him quickly.

“However, even though the Peruman went ahead quickly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, unable to go near Him, also followed very quickly. Just like the proverb, “What is within reach of the hand is not within reach of the mouth,” even though the Nayanar followed the Shiva Peruman, who appeared in front as a disguise, and went quickly to reach Him, he could not reach Him. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman grieved as if he had received nectar in his hand but could not eat it in his mouth.

“Thus, the Lord who went ahead, as if to appear nearby, created a golden temple before him. He created a golden temple before Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, and then entered that golden temple and disappeared. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who had been following the Lord, quickly followed Him and went near that golden temple.

“At the same time, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who had heard the news that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had left the sacred monastery in Thiru-Marai-Kadu, now arrived at the place where this golden temple was located. He came near Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Earlier, the Lord had shown a golden temple to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and then disappeared into that temple. At this same time, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who had left Thiru-Marai-Kadu, arrived at this place. He came very close to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

“At that time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman requested the Lord. O Lord, you called me, saying, “Come,” and showed as if you were coming near, but now you have disappeared. You are not showing yourself to me, who made you open the sacred door without knowing your sacred will. That is very right.

“But Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who sang to close the door, making the power of sacred devotion clear, is now here. How will you show yourself to him now?” Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings.

“Therefore, the worry that he had sung to open the door without knowing the Lord’s sacred will is still in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s sacred heart, which we can understand.

“Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman requests, “You can hide and bless me, who made a mistake, but can you not reveal yourself to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who made no mistake?” Thus, as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman requested, Shiva Peruman, who is still unseen by Vishnu and Brahma, reveals Himself directly to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the king of our Sirkazhi. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman sees that sacred dance, the Lord’s sacred dance, and bows down and praises Him. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman shows that sacred vision of Shiva Peruman to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman so that he can also see it. Earlier, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman had requested Appar Swamigal to sing to open the sacred door.

“Accordingly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sang.

“Now, Shiva Peruman appears to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. When Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman said, “See our Lord,” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman saw Him. When Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman requested, “How can you hide and bless Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman? How can you not appear? How can you not show yourself?” as a result, the Lord appeared and blessed Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

“Thus, as Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman showed, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman saw the sacred vision of Shiva Peruman, the Lord.

“At that time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman composed a Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Paada Adiyaar” (Devotees to sing). Throughout this Thiru-Pathikam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings about seeing the Lord of Thiru-Vaimoor. “I saw the devotees singing, I saw the multitude of devotees, I saw the way He desires the true devotees who stand and speak of the devotion He created, I saw the understanding that kept the mind within.” All these I saw. These are the gifts, he sings in this Thiru-Pathikam. It is the seventy-seventh Thiru-Pathikam in the sixth Thiru-Murai, a Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam.

““I saw the devotees singing and praising, I saw the multitude of devotees, I saw the bustling ghosts dancing and the drums resounding, I saw the fire in His hand, I saw the Ganga in His matted hair that does not dry up, I saw the kokku flower, I saw the konrai flower, I saw a withered skull in His hand, I saw the Lord of Vaimoor as I saw Him.” “I saw a part of Him with a milky voice, I saw the eighteen ganas practicing, I saw the blue-throated neck, I saw the forehead, I saw the bull, I saw the morning sun and moon, I saw the karandai flower appearing on His sacred head, I saw the garland and the matted hair, I saw the Lord of Vaimoor as I saw Him.” “I saw the feet that dance gloriously on the earth, with anklets jingling, I saw the feet that shine in the sky.” Muṭiyum kaṇṭēṉ vēṭampalavāṉ caritai kaṇṭēṉ naṉṉi piriyā maḻuvum kaṇṭēṉ nāḷum maṟaiyaṅkam ōtak kaṇṭēṉ vaṇṇa polintilaṅku kōlam kaṇṭēṉ vāymōr aṭikaḷai nāṉ kaṇṭavārē viḷaitta perumpatti kūṟa niṉṟu meyyaṭiyār tammai virumpa kaṇṭēṉ iḻaikkum katanāka mēṉi kaṇṭēṉ eṇpiṉ kalantikaḻntu tōṇṭa kaṇṭēṉ tiḷaikkum tirumārpil nīṟu kaṇṭēṉ cēṉār matinmūṉṟum poṉṟa aṉṟu vaḷaitta varicilaiyum kaiyil kaṇṭēṉ vāymōr aṭikaḷai nāṉ kaṇṭavārē kāṉmaṟaiyum pōtakat tiṉ urivai kaṇṭēṉ kālil kaḻal kaṇṭēṉ kariyin tōl koṇṭu ūṉmaṟaiyappōrtta vaṭivum kaṇṭēṉ uḷka maṉam vaitta uṇarvum kaṇṭēṉ nāṉmaṟaiyāṉōṭu neṭiyamālum naṉṉi varakkaṇṭēṉ tiṇṇamāka māṉmaṟi taṉ kaiyiṉ maruvak kaṇṭēṉ vāymōr aṭikaḷai nāṉ kaṇṭavārē aṭiyār cilampu vaḻikaḷikaḷ ārpāṇṭēṉ avvarkkē īnta karuṇai kaṇṭēṉ muṭiyār caṭaimēl aṟavam mūḻka mūṟi piṟaipōy maṟaiyak kaṇṭēṉ koṭiyār ataṉmēl iṭapam kaṇṭēṉ kōvaṉamum kīḻum kulāvak kaṇṭēṉ vaṭiyārum mūvilaivēl kaiyil kaṇṭēṉ vāyārum mūvilaivēl kaiyil kaṇṭēṉ vāymōr aṭikaḷai nāṉ kaṇṭavāṟē kuḷaiyār tiruttōṭu kātil kaṇṭēṉ kokkaraiyum caccariyum koḷkai kaṇṭēṉ iḷaiyār poṟinūl valattai kaṇṭēṉ ēḻicaiyāḷ vīṇai muraḷak kaṇṭēṉ talaiyār caṭai kaṇṭēṉ taṉmai kaṇṭēṉ takkaiyoṭu tāḷaṅ karaṅkak kaṇṭēṉ maḻaiyār tirumiṭarum maṟṟum toṭarntu cintippōm tirucciṟṟampalam
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 161 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 423. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. When the Lord, having said “Come to Thiru-Vaimoor,” showed His dance vision, His Thiru-Katchi, near Thiru-Vaimoor to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in turn showed that vision to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, both beheld the Lord’s darshan and sang Tamil garlands of hymns. Earlier, when the Lord had gone ahead and disappeared, saying “Come to Thiru-Vaimoor,” we saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang the Thiru-Kurunthogai, a Thiru-Pathigam, beginning with “Where, what?” Now, having seen the Lord’s vision, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman bestows the Pathigam set to the Nattaraga tune, “Thalirilavalarana Umaipadam.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, having seen the Lord’s vision, sings the Thiru-Thandagam Pathigam, “Paada Adiyar Paravak Kanden.” Thus, three Thiru-Pathigams are dedicated to Thiru-Vaimoor. Having sung thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman worship Lord Shiva, who is enshrined in the Thiru-Vaimoor temple.

This is not the golden temple that the Lord showed and then disappeared from earlier; this is the Thiru-Vaimoor temple. The temple that these two great saints now worshipped is one of the Sapta Vidanga Sthalams located in Thiru-Vaimoor.

Here, the Lord’s sacred name is Vaimoornathar, Vaimoor Adigal. The Goddess’s sacred name is Paalin Nanmozhiyal. The Sthala Vriksham is the Balamaram. The Theertham is Surya Theertham. This is one of the seven Thyagesa Vidanga Sthalams established by Muchukunda Chakravarthy.

Here, Thyagesar, as Neela Vidangar, His dance is the Kamala Nadanam. The Papamega Prachanda Theertham, located opposite the temple, is capable of removing all sins. Brahma and other deities, fearing Tarakaasuran, took the form of birds and wandered. They came to this place, bathed in this Theertham, worshipped the Lord, and were blessed with the removal of their sins. This Theertham holds that glory. In this Sthalam too, in the central mandapam, the Navagrahas are arranged in a single line.

Eight Ashtabhairavas, equivalent to those in Kasi, are said to have been present in this Sthalam: Ananda Bhairavar, Aghora Bhairavar, Utthanda Bhairavar, Bala Bhairavar, Pathala Bhairavar, Eeswara Bhairavar, Kala Bhairavar, and Swarna Bhairavar. However, currently, only four forms are present: Aghora Bhairavar, Ananda Bhairavar, Utthanda Bhairavar, and Bala Bhairavar. In place of the other four Bhairava forms, four Andas have been invoked and installed. Jayantan, the son of Indra, whose curse was removed by Bhairava’s grace, prayed to the Lord of this Sthalam, asking that whoever worships Him on the first Friday of the Chithirai month should have their wishes fulfilled and be granted good grace and progeny.

The Lord granted his wish. Accordingly, every year on the first Friday of the Chithirai month, Jayantan Puja is performed for Bhairava. A Rajagopuram with three tiers faces east. It is built with one prakaram. In front of the Rajagopuram entrance are the Kodi Maram, Bali Peetam, and Nandi Mandapam. Thiru-Vaimoor Sthalam is the third of the Sapta Vidanga Sthalams dedicated to Thyagarajar.

The Thyagarajar shrine is located to the right, on the south side, of the Moolavar Vaimoornathar shrine. To the left of the Moolavar shrine, the Thiru-Maraikkadu Vedharanyeswarar shrine is located. At the entrance of the Moolavar shrine, Dvarapalakas are seen on both sides. The Moolavar Vaimoornathar is enshrined facing east in the sanctum sanctorum. On the birth of the Aippasi month, special Abhishekam and Aradhanas are performed for Neela Vidanga Peruman. To the west of the village is the Surya Theertham, believed to have been created by the sun.

Thus, both great saints have sung and praised the Vaimoor Nathar of this Sthalam and bestowed Pathigams. However, not all of those Pathigams are available to us. As we saw earlier, three Thiru-Pathigams for this Sthalam have been found. These include the Pathigams sung when they saw the golden temple shown by the Lord, and the Pathigam sung before that.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped the Lord, stay together in Thiru-Vaimoor. The two great saints, who were deeply devoted and constantly contemplated the grace of Lord Shiva, had previously stayed together in a Thiru-Madam in Thiru-Maraikkadu.

At that time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, not knowing the Lord’s divine will, felt that he had erred by making a request contrary to Lord Shiva’s divine will and singing a Pathigam, and thus considered himself alienated from divine grace.

Therefore, he withdrew and stayed apart from the devotees, as we saw.

Now, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has received divine indications and experienced a vision of grace. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who were embraced by the Lord’s grace in Thiru-Vaimoor, are now with Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Realizing this, and having now received divine indications and a vision of grace, he is freed from the fear that his previous thought was an error. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s love for the Lord grows ever stronger, and he sings more Pathigams. Currently, he is staying in the same Thiru-Madam with Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in Thiru-Vaimoor for some time. After staying together in the same Thiru-Madam in Thiru-Vaimoor for some time, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman praise the Lord by worshipping the feet of Thiru-Vaimoor Peruman and offering garlands of hymns.

Then, both great saints return to Thiru-Maraikkadu. They humbly worship the Lord of Thiru-Maraikkadu, the Primal Being, and perform sacred services there. They are seated there.

At that time, messengers sent by the faultless and virtuous Pandimadeviyar Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti, the daughter of the Chola king and queen of the Pandya king, and by Kulachiraiyar, the great minister who served before Pandimadevi, come to Vedharanyam to see Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. They arrive at the Thiru-Madam where Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is staying. “Adhi Muthalvar Thamai Panindhu Angu Aana Pani Seidhu Amaru Naal Seethamathi Venkudai Valavar Magalaar Thennan Theviyaar Kothil Gunathu Pandimadeviyaar Mun Kulachiraiyaar Pothavittar Silar” Vandhar Pugazhi Vendhar Thamai Kaana, thus the Peruman composes the song. In this song, the Cholas are referred to by the epithet “Seethamathi Venkudai Valavar.” This means the Cholas who possess the white umbrella, which cools and removes fear from this world, signifying their reign. They are those who do not deviate from righteous rule and possess compassion.

That compassionate rule is honored as the white royal umbrella. Such are the glorious Cholas, whom Sekkizhar Peruman refers to as “Valavar” in this sacred song. “Valavar” means those who possess the wealth of a country that does not need to depend on other nations. Such is the glory of the Cholas, and as their daughter, Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, Pandimadeviyar, was born and lives. She is the daughter of the Cholas and the queen of the Pandya king, Thennan. She is the faultless and virtuous Pandimadeviyar.

This is the first time in the Periya Puranam that Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar is mentioned. Mangaiyarkkarasi Deviyar is one of the sixty-three Nayanmars. This is the first place in the Periya Puranam where she is mentioned.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman praises Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, saying, “Valavar Magalaar Thennan Theviyaar Kothil Gunathu Pandimadeviyar.” Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman’s praise of Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar here reminds us of Mangaiyarkkarasi. The Thevaram composed by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Valavarkon Paavai Varivalai Kaimada Maani Pankayach Chelvi Pandimadevi,” is recalled here. Pandimadeviyar, Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, is the Queen of the Pandya kingdom. Kulachiraiyar, the great minister who serves before her, is also one of the sixty-three Nayanmars. Messengers sent by these two great individuals arrive at Vedharanyam to meet Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the King of Pugazhi. These messengers, who have arrived, possess the qualities of those who have mastered the art of diplomacy.

We will see their character, words, and deeds in detail in the Puranam of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, in this very place.

Now, even though Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman are staying together in the same Thiru-Madam in Vedharanyam, Pandimadeviyar and Kulachirai Nayanar have sent messengers to meet Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, the messengers have come to see Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Having arrived at the Thiru-Madam of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in Thiru-Maraikkadu, they convey their message to the gatekeepers. The gatekeepers take the message, go inside the Thiru-Madam, and inform Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, hearing the news, graciously and joyfully instructs them to invite the messengers inside.

Accordingly, the messengers enter and stand before Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman inquires of the messengers, “Are you free from harm?” That is, he asks if they are without any evil. Generally, people inquire about well-being, asking if one is well.

However, being free from evil is essential for being well.

Therefore, those who ask about well-being will inquire if one is free from evil. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman inquires in this manner. Upon hearing this, the messengers say to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Theedhum Ulaamo Indha Ulagam Uyya Vandheer Iruthaal Ninaivu.” They say, “O Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, no harm will ever come to those who meditate upon your sacred feet, anywhere, at any time.” They further state to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “You have come for the salvation of this world.” The purpose of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s avatar is the refutation of other religions and the establishment of the true one. This is what the messengers convey. They say, “You have come for the salvation of this world, and therefore, no harm will come to those who meditate upon your sacred feet.” The implication of this is that even if we have experienced harm until now, we have meditated upon your sacred feet.

Therefore, any harm that may have existed will no longer remain. Your Holiness must grace our country with your presence. This is what we request and submit to you. The messengers convey this, implying that our Queen, Pandimadeviyar, and the great minister, Kulachiraiyar, are constantly meditating upon your sacred feet. The point here is that meditating upon the sacred feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is the means, and freedom from harm is the benefit.

Our reflection on this continues. Thiru- We pray that you will come to our country. We make this request to you. The messengers convey this, implying that our Queen, Pandimadeviyar, and the great minister, Kulachiraiyar, are constantly meditating upon your sacred feet. The point here is that meditating upon the sacred feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is the means, and freedom from harm is the benefit.

Let us resume our reflection on this. Thiru- Thiruchitrambalam

Chapter 162 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 424. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Messengers sent from the Pandya kingdom by Pandimadeviyar Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar arrive at Vedharanyam and stand before Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. They convey the message given by Pandimadeviyar and Kulachirai Nayanar, requesting him to grace the Pandya kingdom with his presence. The messengers further state that they cannot tolerate the cruel actions of the Jains, who are skilled in falsehood and proclaim their erroneous path as the true path, while the Shaivite path, as expounded in the Vedas, stands firm and unblemished in the world.

They say, the messengers state. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman inquires of the messengers about their well-being, asking if there is any harm or evil. Even though Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman asked, it would not be auspicious to immediately say, “Yes, we have harm.” Therefore, they begin by asking Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Is there any harm to those who meditate on your two sacred feet?” and then proceed to explain the harm they are experiencing.

Thus, these messengers, instead of immediately stating inauspicious news, begin auspiciously and then convey the true message. This is the act of wise people. This is the action of wise people.

Similarly, later, when Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arrived in Madurai, Kulachirai Nayanar, upon greeting and worshipping Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman at the border of Madurai, was asked by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Is the grace and goodness for the Queen and for you abundant?” To which Kulachirai Nayanar replied, “By the great grace of your arrival today, we are eternally blessed with divine grace.” We can recall this incident here as well. We will examine this history in detail in the Puranam of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, the message conveyed by the messengers was that the Shaivite path, as expounded in the Vedas, should flourish in the Pandya kingdom, and the erroneous Jain path should be eradicated from the Pandya kingdom. They were experiencing immense suffering due to the Jains. This was the request the messengers made to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. The Shaivite path is mentioned in the Vedas. The Jain path is a path contrary to the Vedas, an erroneous path. The Vaidika Shaivite path is faultless.

The Jain path, however, is full of faults. The Jain path was considered a high penance, characterized by faults such as plucking hair, torturing the body by lying on hot rocks, and daring to commit murder disguised under the principle of non-violence.

Thus, the messengers made their request to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, asking for the eternal flourishing of the ancient Shaivite path and the removal of the cruelties of the Jains, through the divine sacred ash. the Pandya kingdom should be rid of the Jain path. We are suffering greatly due to the Jains. This was the request the messengers made to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. The Shaivite path is that which is mentioned in the Vedas. The Jain path is a path contrary to the Vedas, an erroneous path. The Vaidika Shaivite path is faultless.

The Jain path, however, is full of faults. The Jain path was considered a high penance, characterized by faults such as plucking hair, torturing the body by lying on hot rocks, and daring to commit murder disguised under the principle of non-violence.

Thus, the messengers made their request to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, asking for the eternal flourishing of the ancient Shaivite path and the removal of the cruelties of the Jains, through the divine sacred ash. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arose, relying on the strength of the sacred ash. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arose, believing that this sacred ash would cause the conversion of Jainism and the flourishing of Shaivism. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arose with mental resolve, thinking that the sacred ash would accomplish these deeds. He sang in the Thiru-Pathikam, “Veyuru Thozhibangan,” that the sacred ash of the Lord, who defeats the Jains and Buddhists in debate, is indeed righteous and firm. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman now made this resolve in his sacred heart.

Similarly, through the Thiru-Neetru Pathikam, Jainism was eradicated in the Pandya kingdom, and Shaivism flourished.

Thus, the messengers’ When Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, listening to the appeal, resolved to go to the Pandya kingdom, remove Jainism, and establish Shaivism, Vageesa Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, conveyed a message to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman said to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “The Jains are very cruel and evil. They are skilled in deceit, not washing the dirt from their bodies, and have done many evil deeds to me in the past.

“Therefore, my child, I will not consent to your going there.” Thus spoke Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. He says that Jains accumulate dirt on their bodies. Jain gurus do not bathe or wash their bodies.

“Therefore, they wander in the sun, sweating, and do not brush their teeth, fearing that worms might die. They follow many such practices, allowing dirt to accumulate on their bodies. They are evil-natured, cruel enough to commit murder, deceitful, and follow wicked deeds, portraying falsehood as truth. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman says all this, adding that these Jains have previously harmed him.

“However, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is not saying all this out of anger or He did not speak out of astonishment. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman did not say these things out of anger, astonishment, or other evil qualities. “It is good to forget what is not good immediately” is a Kural, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was an embodiment of it. The Jains had inflicted many harms upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. They put him in a burning hot chamber, made an elephant trample him, gave him poisoned food, tied him to a stone, and threw him into the sea. Even when the Jains inflicted such harms upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, he remained a compassionate being.

“Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was a being of grace, never showing the slightest anger towards the Jains. But those harms, Why does he mention all those harms to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman here? It is due to the immense affection and love that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar had for Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. He recounts these incidents out of love, so that such harms should not befall Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

“Therefore, we must clearly understand that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar did not say all this based on evil qualities like anger or astonishment.

“Furthermore, when Appar Swamigal says, “I will not consent to your going to a country where such cruel Jains reside,” it is a command of grace, born of the right that Appar Swamigal felt over Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman addresses Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as “Appar” (father) and considers him as such.

“Accordingly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, out of love for Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman whom he considers his child, says, “I will not consent to your going to the Pandya kingdom, that country filled with Jains.” This incident occurred at Thiru-Maraikkadu. When Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having conveyed the message from the people of the Pandya kingdom to Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal from within the great gopuram, was about to take leave, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman spoke these words to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. This event is elaborated in the Puranam of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. We are about to see this. When Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman said that he would not consent to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman going to the Pandya kingdom, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman replied, “I have the intention to go and see the two great souls who praise the boundless sacred ash. I will do nothing but destroy the state of the evil Jains there and spread the Shaiva path.

“This is my oath to you.” Thus, Peruman composes the song here. He says to Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, “I intend to go to the Pandya kingdom and see the two great souls, Pandi Maadeviyar and Kulachirai Nayanar, who praise the boundless sacred ash.

“There, I will destroy the evil Jains and their ways. He says, “I will destroy the state of the Jains who commit evil deeds and foster the Shaiva path. I will do no other deed. This is my oath to you,” says Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman to Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal. He says he will destroy the state of the Jains and promote the Shaiva religion. The purpose of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s incarnation is to refute other religions and make the glory of the sacred ash manifest.

“He places both these objectives here and replies to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. He says, “Devotees who recite the garland of sacred words will rule in heaven. This is our command,” as he declares with an oath in the eleventh verse of the Kol-Aru Pathikam. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman sings with an oath in the Thiru-Nanippalli Thevaram, “Thinking of Thiru-Nanippalli, karma will be destroyed; this is our command.” We can see such declarations with an oath in the sacred utterances of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

“Here, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who sings with such oaths, says to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, “This is your command.” This is because Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar had commanded, “My child, I will not consent to your going.” Therefore, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s reply implies, “I will not go by contradicting you. I will go according to your command. My going is for this sacred service, to change the state of Jainism and make Shaivism flourish. May your command support this.” Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman replies, implying that he seeks support. When Appar Swamigal, standing in the position of Appar, said he would not consent, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, standing in the position of a child, replied to Appar Peruman as a child.

“This is the point here.

“Furthermore, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman continues to tell Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, “You need not come with me. You stay here. I alone will go to the Pandya kingdom, change the state of the Jains, and establish Shaivism.” He takes leave of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, implying that after eradicating the state of Jainism and establishing Shaivism, he will return here to see him again. From Thiru-Pukalur, these two great souls began their pilgrimage and have, until now, journeyed together for a long time through many sacred places. They have traveled together, visiting sacred sites and composing sacred hymns for the world’s well-being.

“Now, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who is about to embark on the pilgrimage to the Pandya kingdom, states that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar need not accompany him, and that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar should remain at Thiru-Maraikkadu, while he alone will go to the Pandya kingdom to remove the evil of the Jains and make Shaivism flourish. Why does he say this? These two, who have journeyed together from Thiru-Pukalur until now, could continue to the Pandya kingdom. Why does Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman tell Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, “You stay here”? Sivakavimani Aiyya explains Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred intention as follows: Pandi Maadeviyar and Kulachiraiyar sent messengers to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, conveying their message.

“Therefore, it would be most appropriate for Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman alone to go to the Pandya kingdom, in accordance with their request. This is because Pandi Maadeviyar and Kulachirai Nayanar had sent messengers specifically requesting Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman to come to the Pandya kingdom.

“Next, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s journey to the Pandya kingdom is for the purpose of eradicating the arrogance of the alien religion, Jainism, and for the flourishing of Vaidika Shaiva Siddhanta. These two objectives are the very purpose of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred incarnation.

“Therefore, it is fitting that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman alone should perform these deeds, which are the very essence of his incarnation.

“Now, thirdly, when an evil arises, one way is to internalize it, remain calm, and do nothing against it, allowing its power to diminish. The second way is to confront that evil, attack it, and remove it. During this period, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman incarnated and lived, the evils of alien religions like Jainism and Buddhism were widespread throughout the Tamil country at that time. They afflicted and prevented the flourishing of Shaiva enlightenment. It was the Lord’s sacred will to remove these evils by both the methods mentioned above and to show it to the world.

“The Lord demonstrates, through Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, the method of doing nothing against evil and allowing its power to diminish. He is about to demonstrate, through Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the method of confronting evil, attacking it, and destroying it. We can recall here how Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman endured all the evils committed by the Jains, overcame them, and converted the Pallava king to the Shaiva religion.

“Now, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman goes to the Pandya kingdom, debates with the Jains, opposes them, and removes them. This is the second method of confronting and destroying evil, which Lord Shiva demonstrates. We can see this. From the upcoming history, that is, from the upcoming history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and further from the history of Pazhaiyarai Vadathali that will occur later, Lord Shiva, who desired to show it to the world, thus willed to send only Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman to the Pandya kingdom.

“Now, fourthly, if Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar had also gone to the Pandya kingdom with Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and removed the evil deeds committed by the Jains, then the history would record that two Shaiva acharyas came to remove the evils of Jainism. This would lead to the accusation that the Shaiva religion needed two acharyas to remove the evils of Jainism. This would diminish the glory of both these great acharyas.

“Therefore, to demonstrate that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman alone is sufficient to remove the evils of the Jains, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman goes to the Pandya kingdom.

“Next, fifthly, if both great souls had gone together and eradicated the Jain evil there, the world would not have been able to clearly understand and follow who eradicated the Jain evil, and would have been confused. To avoid this, Peruman acts in this manner, performing this sacred play.

“Now, sixthly, even if Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had been invited, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who had spoken about the deceptive cunning and evils of the Jains and refused to let Pillaiyar go there, would have preferred to stay away from the place where those evil Jains resided, in accordance with the rule that “seeing evil people is also evil.” This is the sixth reason.

“Now, seventhly, even if Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman wished to avoid approaching the Jains, he would have agreed to accompany Peruman when he went.

“Therefore, to clarify this, Pillaiyar resolved to go to the Pandya kingdom alone.

“Thus, in seven ways, Siva- Kavimani Aiyya explains the seven reasons why Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman alone went to the Pandya kingdom.

“Thus, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having said this and taken leave of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, proceeds to the Tamil country, the Pandya kingdom. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Pandya kingdom as Tamil Nadu in this verse, speaking of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the leader of wisdom. Although Tamil Nadu can be understood as the country where Tamil-speaking people reside, our sages have referred to the Pandya kingdom as Tamil Nadu. There were many countries where Tamil was spoken, such as Thondai Nadu, Nadu Nadu, Chola Nadu, Kongu Nadu, Chera Nadu, etc. Nevertheless, due to the special significance of the Pandya kingdom, if Tamil Nadu is used as a proper noun, it refers to the Pandya kingdom. This is because Lord Shiva, the primordial God, presided over the Sangam and fostered Tamil.

“The Pandya kingdom possesses the Podhigai Hills, where the Tamil sage Agathiyar still resides. Due to these many reasons, if Tamil Nadu is used as a proper noun, it refers to the Pandya kingdom.

“Therefore, all our sages have referred to the Pandya kingdom as Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu refers to the Pandya kingdom.
