Researchers state that names like Silaippalli, Silappalli, and Chirappalli arose from the meaning of ‘Palli’ (temple) carved into stone. This site stands prominently in the center of Thiru-Chirappalli, visible from anywhere in the city.

The Lord enshrined on the hill is known by names such as Sevvanthinathar, Thirumalai Kozhundhar, and Thayu-Manavar. In Sanskrit, the Swami is called Mathrubhuteswarar. The Amman’s sacred name is Sugandha Kunthalambikai, and in Tamil, Mattuvar Kuzhal Ammai. This mountain also has the name Thirumalai.

Therefore, the Lord is also known by the sacred name Thirumalai Perumanadigal, and this city is known as Chittambar. It is understood that since Sarama Munivar worshipped with Sevvanthi flowers, the Lord is called Sevvanthinathar. Because He is the sprout of the mountain, He is called Thirumalai Kozhundeesar. And because He came as a mother to help a woman out of love, He is called Thayu-Manavar. The local Vinayagar is called Sevvanthi Vinayagar. The Manikka Vinayagar shrine at the base of the temple is very famous.

Now, regarding the sacred waters associated with this temple: Kaveri, Sivagangai, Somarohini (also known as Brahma Theertham), Nandrudaiyan Theertham, Theeyathillan Theertham, and others. The Kaveri, which flows north of the town, is the Kudakavari. The Thiru-Pugal hymns, such as “Neelalai Soodiya Thiru-Chiramalai Mel Urai Veera,” inform us that the Kaveri flowed near the mountain in ancient times. Next is Sivagangai, which is located near the Naganatha Swamy Temple to the northwest of the temple. It is said that Ambikai performed penance here to marry the Lord. Next is Somarohini, also called Brahma Theertham.

It is a beautiful temple tank with a central mandapam, located on the western side of the temple. It was built by Viswanatha Nayakkar, who formerly ruled Thiru-Chi. Next is Nandrudaiyan Theertham, which is a short distance east of the temple, near the present Thiru-Chi railway station. Next is Theeyathillan Theertham, located south of the temple. The sixth day of the festival takes place. One can see that Thiru-Gnana Sambandha Peruman, in the first verse of his Thevaram for this site, placed these sacred waters, praised as Nandrudaiyan and Theeyathillan, within the hymn.

This site is called Dakshina Kailasa. It is called Dakshina Kailasa. From the bottom to the Swami shrine, the paths are covered. The Swami temple above the Amman temple is built as a multi-storied structure. Every year, on the 23rd, 24th, and 25th days of the Panguni month, the rays of the evening sun shine directly on the Moolalingam. This is called Surya Pooja.

There are two cave temples carved into the rock, both on and below the hill. In the upper cave, there are many inscriptions in Grantha and Tamil. There are many literary works about this site. The mountain is situated in the middle of the city, arranged so that anyone looking can have a darshan. In Sangam literature, this mountain is praised as Nedum Perungundram. In Agananooru, it is mentioned as “Karangisai Vizhavin Urandai Gunathu Nedum Perungundram.” According to the Purana, Of the three, Murthi (Deity), Sthalam (Holy Place), and Theertham (Sacred Water), Thiruvarur is especially renowned.

The liberation attained by being born in Thiruvarur, and the blessings easily obtained by merely uttering the name of this holy place, are affirmed by the sacred words of Appar Swamigal, who stated that even uttering its name with devotion dispels evil deeds. Those who circumambulate the hill on the auspicious days of Chithirai month’s beginning and end, and on the Poora Nakshatram and Navami Thithi, will receive their desired boons. On the auspicious day of Somavaram (Monday) combined with Rohini Nakshatram, and for those who bathe in Brahma Theertham and worship in Panguni month, all benefits will be bestowed. Those who bathe in Sivagangai on Purattasi Pournami, offer Thumbai flowers to the Lord, and worship Him, will attain a good life.

Once upon a time, the Devas came to worship Lord Shiva, who resides on Thiru-Kailashagiri.

At that time, Adiseshan arrived, and everyone praised and celebrated him. Witnessing this, Vayu Devan became extremely jealous and began to speak ill of Adiseshan. Subsequently, a competition arose between the two, asking: “Who is greater? Who is more powerful?” Adiseshan tightly bound Mount Kailash with his body. Vayu Devan began to blow wind with all his might, causing the entire world to tremble.

At that moment, three fragments broke off from Mount Kailash; one fell in Thiru-Kalaathi, another in Thiru-Siramalai, and the third in Thiru-Konamalai in Lanka. As these were fragments of Thiru-Kailashamalai, these three became known as Then-Kailash (Southern Kailash). Among these, Thiru-Siramalai holds greater significance as it is centrally located between Thiru-Kalaathi and Thiru-Konamalai.

Now, the sacred history of the Lord here, known as Mathrubhootheswarar and Thayumanavar Swamy: In the Chola kingdom, in Kaveripoompattinam, a merchant named Rathinagupthan, born into a merchant family, lived a domestic life with his chaste wife. By the grace of the Lord, he was blessed with a daughter named Rathinavathi. Rathinagupthan arranged the marriage of his daughter, Rathinavathi, to Thanagupthan, a merchant residing in Thiru-Siramalai.

Thus, Rathinavathi lived in Thiru-Siramalai with her husband, Thanagupthan. From the very first day she arrived in Thiru-Siramalai from Thiru-Kaveri-Poompattinam, Rathinavathi unfailingly and lovingly worshipped Sevvandhinathan. In due course, by the grace of the Lord of Siramalai, Rathinavathi became pregnant and reached the time of delivery. Hearing this news, Rathinavathi’s mother, who was in Kaveripoompattinam, set out with the necessary medicines, oils, and other provisions for her daughter.

At that time, the Kaveri River was heavily flooded.

Therefore, the Kaveri flood prevented Rathinavathi’s mother from reaching her daughter for the delivery. The daughter kept thinking, “My mother will come today, she will come tomorrow, she will bring the things I need.” The time of delivery drew near, but her mother did not arrive. At this moment, Rathinavathi prayed to Thiru-Siramalai Sevvandhinathar, whom she had been worshipping.

The Lord Shiva, known as Sankaran, Sivan, Sadashivan, Eesan, Eesanan, Pungavan, Thirupuranthakan, Puraathanan, Puraanan, Gangai Nayagan, Karaimidatru Irai, Nuthal Kannaan, our Lord, Iraamaiyan, the Lord of Siramalai, Pooranan, Paran, Paraparan, Velliyamporuppan, Kaaranan, Madananthakan, Kaalanai Kadindhon, Vaaranan thanai urithavan, Maraiporul Vaguthon, Naaranan thanakku ariyavan, the Lord of Siramalai, Lord Shiva, assumed the guise of Rathinavathi’s mother and arrived at Rathinavathi’s house, where she was suffering from labor pains. The daughter, too, rejoiced, believing the newcomer to be her mother. The mother and student, Lord Shiva, performed the necessary treatments. Rathinavathi had a smooth delivery, and a beautiful baby boy was born. The one who came as the mother stayed for a few days, protecting both the child and the mother. While this was happening, the flood in the Kaveri receded, and Rathinavathi’s real mother crossed the river and arrived at Rathinavathi’s house.

Rathinavathi was astonished when she saw her. She wondered how there could be two mothers. Immediately, Thayumanavar Swamy, Lord Shiva, who had come as the mother, disappeared and appeared in the sky on His Rishabha Vahanam (bull mount).

From that day onwards, the sacred name Thayumanavar became permanently associated with Siramalai Sevvandhinathar. Rathinavathi, too, having worshipped the Lord, shines even today as one of His devotees. This history is celebrated grandly on the fifth day of the temple’s Brahmotsavam.

Now, the history of the Lord facing west here: A sage named Saramamunivar established a Nandavanam (flower garden) for the Lord of Siramalai, cultivating Sevvandhi flowers brought from Naga Lokam, and daily worshipped the Lord with these flowers. During the reign of Paranthaka Chozhan in Uraiyur, also known as Kozhiyur, a flower merchant entered the sage’s Nandavanam, stole Sevvandhi flowers, and presented them to the king’s queen.

One day, the sage observed this secretly and reported it to the king. The king did not reprimand the merchant.

Therefore, the sage complained to the Lord.

The Lord of Siramalai turned His face from east to west. He caused a rain of mud to fall in Uraiyur with many clouds. The king and his pregnant wife had gone out. Uraiyur was destroyed by the mud rain. The mud rain continued to follow the king. Finally, the king died, falling into the Kaveri.

The queen, Bhuvanamadevi, who had fallen and escaped, was rescued by a Brahmin and gave birth to a baby boy. This child later became known as Karikal Chozhan.

Now, the history of Thanthonreesar: Jananatha Chozhan, born in the lineage of Manu, had a son named Suravathitha Chozhan. He ruled from Uraiyur, which was named Kozhiyur because a hen had defeated an elephant there.

One day, the Chozhan went hunting near Saramamunivar’s Nandavanam.

At that time, seven Naga maidens, daughters of Adiseshan, were going to worship Siramalainathar with Sevvandhi flowers. The king saw them and wished to marry them. They did not consent. The king went to Naga Lokam, obtained Adiseshan’s consent, married Kanthimathi among the maidens, received a Shiva Lingam and a sword from Adiseshan, and returned to his city. He consecrated the Lingam he had brought and performed worship. Kanthimathi, the Chozhan’s wife, out of intense devotion, obtained her husband’s permission and daily walked to Thiru-Siramalainathar to worship Him.

In due course, Kanthimathi became pregnant, and even during her pregnancy, she unfailingly visited the Lord.

One day, due to the sun’s heat, she became too weak to walk and fell on the way. She grieved, thinking that she would not be able to have darshan today. Immediately, Siramalainathar appeared as a Swayambhu Lingam at that spot and gave darshan to Kanthimathi. Since the Lord appeared as a Swayambhu, He was named Thanthonreeswarar. Kanthimathi praised the Lord in many ways and returned to her city. Her husband, Suravathithan, hearing of this miracle, built a separate temple for Thanthonreeswarar and arranged for worship to be performed.

This temple is on the road leading to Uraiyur.

Now, the history of the marriage of Mattuvar Kuzhali Ammai: Goddess Uma, desiring to worship Lord Shiva and marry Him, appeared in this holy place in the form of a small girl from a lotus flower and was raised by Sage Kathiyayana. As the Goddess’s hair naturally exuded a good fragrance, she was called Sugandha Kunthalambikai and Mattuvar Kuzhali. The Goddess bathed in the Theertham called Sivagangai and worshipped the Swayambhu Lingam that appeared nearby, performing penance. This place is known as Naganatha Swamy Temple. The Lord, intending to fulfill her original desire, appeared and gave darshan to the Goddess and married her. This marriage festival takes place on the sixth day of the Chithirai festival.

Now, the history of Thayumanavar Adigal: In the Chola kingdom, in Thirumarai Kadu, also known as Vedharanyam, about three hundred years ago, a Saiva Vellalar named Kediliyappillai lived. He served the government in Thiruchirappalli. Vijayaraghunatha Chokkalinga Nayakkar, having heard of Kediliyappillai’s good qualities, summoned him to Trichy and appointed him to the position of political accountant. While Kediliyappillai was working in Thiruchirappuram, he prayed to the Lord of this place for offspring. He already had a son named Sivachidambaram, but he had given that son in adoption to his elder brother.

Therefore, he prayed to the Lord for a son. He prayed to Thayumanavar Peruman. By the grace of the Lord, a beautiful baby boy was born. He named the child Thayumanavar, after the Lord. Thayumanavar grew up well. His mind was intensely focused on finding a Gnana Guru, receiving good instruction, and freeing himself from the cycle of birth.

He daily worshipped Sri Thayumanavar Peruman with love and devotion.

Then, one day, Mounaguru Swamigal, who belonged to the lineage of Thirumoola Nayanar, was on a pilgrimage and was in a state of samadhi in the Dakshinamurthy shrine in this temple. When Thayumanavar came for darshan as usual, like iron drawn by a magnet, he fell at the feet of Mounaguru, who was in samadhi, and pleaded. Mounaguru, seeing Thayumanavar’s ripened state, imparted spiritual instruction to him. Thayumanavar Swamigal shone as a recipient of Shiva’s experience, singing the song “Anging enaathapadi engum prakasamai aanandhapoorrthiyaagi arulodu nirainthathu ethu” (That which is everywhere, shining, full of bliss, filled with grace, without being here or there). He also gave to the world many sacred verses containing Siddhanta concepts, clarifying that Vedanta’s clarity is Siddhanta.

Therefore, he was known by the names Thayumanavar Adigal and Thayumanavar Swamigal.

Thus, Thayumanavar Swamigal lived a detached life, visited many holy places for darshan, and finally in Lakshmipuram, belonging to Ramanathapuram, he attained the sacred feet of the Lord in Nirvikalpa Samadhi. There is also a temple for Adigal there. His sacred verses are known as Thayumanavar Padalgal. In this temple, there are two cave temples carved out of the hill. One is on the hill and the other at the base. From the markings in the cave temple on the hill, it appears to have been built by the Pallava king Gunaparan, also known as Mahendravarman, who lived in the sixth century.

We have seen in the beginning of the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal that Mahendravarman converted from Jainism to Saivism. This temple has many mandapams from the base to the top. There are the Aayirakkal Mandapam (thousand-pillared hall), Vahana Mandapam, Sahasralinga Mandapam, Noorrukkal Mandapam (hundred-pillared hall), Chithira Mandapam, Pathinaaru Kal Mandapam (sixteen-pillared hall), and Mani Mandapam. The great ones who worshipped the Lord of this holy place and received blessings include Brahma, Agasthiyar, Indra, Uma Devi, Jadayu, the Saptharishis, Thiruchiran, Rama, Arjuna, Hanuman, Vibhishana, the radiant Ayyanaar, Naga Kannigais, Saramamunivar, Vandu Chozhan, Rathinavathi, Mounaguru, and Thayumanavar Swamigal. The Hanuman Mudra worshipped by Hanuman is carved on the hill. It is also said that Agasthiyar, after worshipping here, pressed another equally tall mountain into the netherworld.

The Uchipillaiyar Temple on the mountain peak is very famous. The Mutt of Mouna Swamigal is located in this holy place. The affairs of the Mouna Mutt are still managed by the Dharmapuram Adheenam of the Thiru-Kailaya Paramparai. Daily rituals are performed excellently in this temple. Annually, in the months of Chithirai and Panguni respectively, the Chariot Festival and the Float Festival take place. In Chithirai and Vaikasi, Vasanthotsavams are held on the hill.

In the month of Aadi, a separate Aadi Pooram festival is held for the Goddess. The Sevvandhi Puranam, also known as Thiruchiramalai Puranam, was composed by Saiva Ellappa Navalar. It consists of eleven sections and five hundred and fifty verses. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this holy place, composed one Thiru-Pathigam (decad of verses). It is the eighty-fifth Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Kurunthagai Thiru-Pathigam, in the fifth Thirumurai.

“Mattuvār kuzhalāḷoḍu mālviḍaiyiṭṭa māvukandhu ēṟum iṟaivaṉār kaṭṭu nīttavarkku iṉṉarulē ceyyum ciṭṭar pōlum cirāppaḷḷi celvarē.” (The Lord, who rides the great bull with the fragrant-haired Goddess, seems to be a noble one who bestows sweet grace upon those who have shed their bonds, the wealthy one of Sirappalli.) “Ariyaṉ talai veṭṭivaṭṭāṭiṉār ariyayaṉ tozhuthēttum arumporuḷ periyavaṉ cirāppaḷḷiyai pēṇuvār ariyaṉ tozha aṅkiruppārkaḷē.” (He who cut off the head of Ariyan and played with it, the great essence worshipped by Ariyan and Ayan, those who cherish Sirappalli will be there to worship Ariyan.) “Ariccirāppakal aivarāl āṭṭuṇṭu curiccirāthu neñcē oṉṟu collakkīzh tiruccirāppaḷḷi eṉṟalum tīviṉai nariccirāthu.” (O heart, do not be troubled by the five senses day and night; when one utters ‘Thiruchirappalli’ even once, evil deeds will not approach.) “Naṭakkum naṭakkumē tāyumāy eṉakku ētalai kaṇṇumāy pēyaṉēṉaiyum āṇṭa peruntakai tēyanātaṉ cirāppaḷḷi mēviya nāyaṉār eṉa nam viṉai nācamē.” (He who became my mother, my eye, and ruled over even me, a madman, the great Lord, the Lord of Sirappalli, our Lord, our karma is destroyed.) Only four of these sacred verses have been found; the other six verses are not available to us.

We shall proceed with our reflection.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 174 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 436, Thiru-Nindracharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped Thiru-Chirappalli, reached the holy place called Thiru-Karkudi, also known as Uyyakkondan Malai, on the western border of Thiru-Chirappalli. Uyyakkondan Malai is a temple situated on a small hill. Since the Lord resides on the hill, this place is called Karkudi. To uplift all beings, the Lord here is enshrined by the names Ujjivanathar and Uyyakkondan.

This holy place has been sung by the three great saints: Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. It is the place where Markandeya was blessed. The temple is located on the hill. There are steps from the bottom to the top. At the foot of the hill, there is a Theertham. After worshipping Ganesha at the base and ascending the steps, one reaches the outer circumambulatory path around the temple.

After circumambulating it and ascending further, one can reach the Natarajar Mandapam. The temple has three entrances: two facing south and one facing east. The shrines of the Lord and Goddess face west. There are two shrines for the Goddess; one faces east, and the main Goddess shrine faces west. One can circumambulate here and reach the Lord’s shrine for worship.

The Lord is a Swayambhu Murthi. This temple contains the Pathigam sung by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, praising the various glories of Karkudi Mamalaiyar; the Pathigam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, immersed in the joy of beholding the Lord of Karkudi; and the Pathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, seeking refuge. The Lord’s sacred names are Ujjivanathar, Uyyakkondar, Ujjinathar, Muttheesar, and Karpaganathar. The Goddess’s names are Anjanakshi. The old Goddess shrine faces west. The Theerthams are Ponnoli Odai, Kudamurutti, Gnanavavi, Enkonakkinaru (octagonal well), and Narkonakkinaru (quadrangular well) – five Theerthams in total.

The Sthala Vriksham is the Bilva tree. Upamanyu Muni, Markandeya, Karan, the king of Eelam, and Arunagirinathar have worshipped here. When Markandeya worshipped the Lord in various holy places, upon reaching and worshipping this holy place of Thiru-Karkudi, he completed his sixteenth year. Karan, one of Ravana’s brothers, worshipped the Lord of this place and received His grace. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this holy place, composed a Thiru-Pathigam in praise of the Lord of this place. It is the sixth Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Thandagam Thiru-Pathigam.

“Mooththavaṉai vāṉavarkku mūvā mēṉi mutalvaṉai tiruvaraiyiṉ mūkka pāmpu oṉṟu ārththavaṉai akkaravam āramāka aṇindhavaṉai paṇindhu aṭiyār aṭaindha” (The ancient one, the ageless primal one for the celestials, who bound a snake around his sacred waist, who wore a snake as a garland, whom devotees reached by worshipping him with love). “Aṉpōṭu ēththavaṉai iru varaiyil tēṉai ēṉōrkku iṉṉamudham azhiththavaṉai iṭaraiyellām kāththavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (With love, I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is praised, who gave sweet nectar to those who were not, who protected from all troubles.) “Ceyyāṉai veḷiyāṉai kariyāṉ taṉṉai ticaimukaṉai ticaiyaṭṭum ceṟindāṉ taṉṉai aiyāṉai noyiyāṉai cīriyāṉai aṇiyāṉai cēyāṉai āṉañcāṭum meyyāṉai poyyāthumillāṉ taṉṉai viṭaiyāṉaic caṭaiyāṉai veṟiththa māṉ koḷ kaiyāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is red, who is white, who is black, who is the four-faced one, who pervades all eight directions, who is the master, who is subtle, who is great, who is near, who is far, who is the true one who dances with the five elements, who is without falsehood, who rides the bull, who has matted locks, who holds the frightened deer in his hand.) “Maṇ athaṉil aindhai mā nīril nāṉkai vayaṅkeṟiyil mūṉṟai māruthatthiṉ iraṇṭai viṇ athaṉil oṉṟai virikathirai taṇmathiyai tārakaihaḷ tammiṉmikka eṇ athaṉil ezhuththai ēḻicaiyai kāmaṉ ezhil azhiya eriyumizhndha imaiyā neṟṟik kaṇ avaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the five in earth, the four in great water, the three in shining fire, the two in wind, the one in sky, the spreading rays, the cool moon, the stars, the letter in numbers, the seven notes of music, who emitted fire from his unblinking third eye to destroy Kama’s beauty.) “Naṟṟavaṉai puṟṟaṟavaṉāṉai nāṉāthu nakuthalai ūṉ nayandāṉ taṉṉai muṟṟavaṉai mūvātha mēṉiyāṉai muṉṉīriṉ nañcam ugandhu uṇṭāṉ taṉṉai paṟṟavaṉai paṟṟārtham pathikaḷ ceṟṟa paṭaiyāṉai aṭaivārtham pāvam pōkka kaṟṟavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the good ascetic, who is the ascetic of the anthill, who desired the flesh of the smiling skull without shame, who is complete, who has an ageless body, who gladly consumed the poison from the primordial ocean, who is the one who holds, who has the army that destroyed the cities of his enemies, who is learned in removing the sins of those who approach him.) “Caṅkaithanai tavirththāṇṭa talaivaṉ taṉṉai caṅkaraṉai taḷaluṟu tāḻ mazhu vāḻ tāṅgum aṅkaiyaṉai aṅkamaṇi ākatthāṉai ākatthōr pākatthai amaravaiththa maṅkaiyaṉai mathiyoṭu mācuṉamum tammiṉ maruva viricaṭai muṭimēl vaiththa vāṇīr kaṅkaiyaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the leader who ruled by dispelling doubts, who is Shankara, who holds the sharp axe in his beautiful hand, who has a gem on his body, who placed a part of the maiden in his body, who placed the bright water of the Ganga on his matted locks, along with the moon and the snake, to mingle with each other.) “Peṇṇavaṉai āṇavaṉai pēṭāṉāṉai piṟappiliyai iṟappiliyai pērāvāṇi viṇṇavaṉai viṇṇavarkkum mēlāṉāṉai.” (He who is woman, who is man, who is neither, who is without birth, who is without death, who is the great sky, who is superior even to the celestials.) “Vēthiyaṉai vēthatthiṉ kīthampāṭum paṇṇavaṉai paṇṇil vaṟu payaṉ āṉāṉai pāravaṉai pāril vāḻ uyirkaḷkkellām kaṇṇavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the Vedic scholar, who sings the hymns of the Vedas, who is the fruit of the melody, who is the earth, who is the eye for all living beings on earth.) “Paṇṭāṉai paranthāṉai kuvinthāṉ taṉṉai pārāṉai viṇṇā ivvulakamellām uṇṭāṉai umizhndāṉai uṭaiyāṉ taṉṉai oruvarunthan perumaithanai aṟiyavoṉṉā viṇṭāṉai viṇṭārtham puṟaṅkaḷ mūṉṟum vevvaḻalil venthu poṭiyāki vīḻa kaṇṭāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththaik kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is ancient, who is expansive, who is gathered, who is the earth, who swallowed and spat out all these worlds, who is the owner, whose greatness no one can know, who saw the three cities of his enemies burn to ashes in fierce fire.) “Vāṉavaṉai vāṉavarkku mēlāṉāṉai vaṇaṅgum aṭiyār maṉaththuḷ maruvippukka tēṉavaṉaith tēvar toḻu kaḷalāṉ taṉṉai ceykuṇaṅkaḷ palavāki niṉṟa eṉṟi kōṉavaṉai kollai viṭaiyēṟṟiṉāṉai kuzhal muzhavum iyampa kūtthāṭavalla kāṇavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththaik kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the celestial, who is superior to the celestials, who is the honey that entered the hearts of worshipping devotees, whose feet are worshipped by the Devas, who is the king who stood as many good qualities, who rode the wild bull, who can dance to the sound of the flute and drum.) “Kolaiyāṉai.” “Uripōrththa koḷkaiyāṉai kōḷariyai kūrampā varaimēl kōththa cilaiyāṉai cemmaitharu poruḷāṉ taṉṉai tiripuraththōr mūvarkku cemmai ceytha talaiyāṉai thatthuvaṅkaḷ āṉāṉ taṉṉai taiyalōr paṅkiṉaṉai taṉ kai ēnthu kalaiyāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who has the nature of wearing the skin of a murderous elephant, who is the bow strung with a sharp arrow on the mountain, who is the substance that gives righteousness, who is the head who brought righteousness to the three in Thirupuram, who became the Tattvas, who has a maiden as a part of himself, who holds the crescent moon in his hand.) “Pozhilāṉai pozhilārum puṉkūṟāṉai puṟampayaṉai aṟampurindha pukalūrāṉai ezhilāṉai iṭaimeruthiṉ iṭam koṇṭāṉai īṅkōy nīṅkāthu uṟaiyum iṟaivaṉ taṉṉai azhalāṭu mēṉiyaṉai aṉṟu ceṉṟa kuṉṟaṭuththa aṟakkaṉ tōl neṟiya ūṉṟum kaḷalāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the grove, who is the one with the grove of Pungoor, who is Purambayan, who is the Lord of Pukalur who performed righteousness, who is beautiful, who took his place in the middle of the Marudha tree, who is the Lord who resides in Eengoy without leaving, who has a body that dances with fire, whose foot pressed down the skin of the demon who approached the mountain that day.) 

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped Thiru-Karkudi, reached the holy place called Thiru-Parayathurai. This is one of the holy places on the southern bank of the Kaveri. On the banks of rivers, we can see many holy places that shine with the name ‘Thurai’ (ford/bank). Since the Lord is enshrined amidst the Parai tree groves on the bank of the Kaveri, it is called Parayathurai. The Parai tree is the Sthala Vriksham of this place. This tree is located in the western prakaram of the temple.

In Sanskrit, it is called Tharuga Vriksham. It is said that the shade of this tree is excellent for performing penance. It was formerly known as Tharugavanam, and it is associated with the history of the Lord going as Bhikshatana to Tharugavanam, removing the ego of the sages, and giving them darshan. It is located on the Thiruchirappalli-Karur road. The shrine faces east. Adjacent to the seven-tiered gopuram, which houses the Panchamurthis, there is a Vasantha Mandapam.

There is a small sacred pond. Adjacent to the mandapam, a seven-tiered gopuram adorns the temple. Passing through the gopuram entrance, one enters the Nandi Mandapam. In the first prakaram, there are the sixty-three Nayanmars, and subsidiary deities such as Vinayagar, Murugan, Mahalakshmi, and Durga, as well as the Navagrahas. In the Garbhagriha Koshtams, Dakshinamurthy and Ardhanareeswarar are present. The Lord’s shrine faces east, and the Goddess’s shrine faces south.

The Goddess’s shrine is in the Mahamandapam. The Panchamurthis are enshrined in the Snapana Mandapam. The Lord’s name here is Tharugavaneswarar, and in Tamil, Parayathurainathar. The Goddess’s name is Hemavarnambikai, and in Tamil, Pasum Pon Mayilammai. The Theertham is the Kaveri River. On the first day of Aippasi, the Lord, mounted on His Rishabha Vahanam, along with the Goddess, bestows Theertham in the Kaveri.

In inscriptions, this place is referred to as Utthamaseevi Chathurvedi Mangalathu Thiruparayathurai, and the Lord’s name as Parayathurai Mahadevar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang one Thiru-Pathigam and Appar Swamigal rendered one Thiru-Pathigam for this Thalam, which is also referred to as Paraythurai Parameswaran. Manikkavasaga Peruman praised the Peruman of this Thalam in Thiruvasagam, Thiru-Agaval, saying, “Paraythurai Meviya Parane Potri.” In the fourth Thiru-Padal of Thiruvasagam Sethilapathu, he praised the Peruman of this Thalam as “Then Paraythuraiyai Sivaloka.” Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this Thalam, rendered a Thiru-Pathigam, which is the thirtieth Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thirumurai, structured as a Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam.

Karappar Kalam Adainthavar Tham Vinai Surukkumaru Vallar Gangai Senjadai Parappu Neervaru Kaveri Thenkarai Thirupparaythurai Meviya Selvare Mudinar Kali Yanaiyin Iruri Padinar Marai Nankinodu Aram. Sedanar Thenparaythurai Selvarai Thedik Kondu Adiyen Sendru Kanbene. Pattanetriyir Palmathikkitrinar Nattamaduvar Nallirul Emamum Sittanar Then Paraythurai Selvanar Ittamayirupparai Arivare. Munbelan Sila Molaimai Pesuvar Enbellam Pala Poondangulitharvar Thenparaythurai Meviya Selvanar Anbaray Irupparai Arivare. Podu Thathodu Kondu Punaithuvudan Thathavizh Sadai Sankaran Pathathul Vathai Theerkka Venrethip Paraythurai Sothiyanai Thozhuthu Ezhunthu Uyamine.

Nalla Nanmarai Othiya Nambanai Pallil Venthalaiyil Palikolvanai Thillaiyan Thenparaythurai Selvanai Vallaiyay Vanangi Thozhuvaymaiye. Neruppinar Kuvithalokku Nezh Sadai Paruppatham Matha Yanai Urithavan Thirupparaythuraiyar Thirumarbin Nool Porupparavi Izhu. Thulippunal Pondrathe. Ettavitta Idumanekkar Mel Patta Nunthuli Payum Paraythurai Sittan Sevadi Sendradaiyitrel Vittu Nam Vinai Ullana Vidume. Nerupparay Nimirthalokku Nezhsadai Marupparay Valaithalokkum Vanmathi Thirupparaythurai Meviya Selvanar Virupparayirupparai Arivare. Thondu Padiyum Thoomalar Thooviyum Indai Katti Inaiyadi Ethiyum Pandarangar Paraythurai Pangaraik Kandukondadiyen Uynthu Povane.

Arakkan Atral Azhitha Azhaganai Parakku Neer Ponni Mannu Paraythurai Irukkai Meviya Isanai Ethu Meen Porukka Num Vinai Poyarunganinai.

Thodarnthu Sinthippom.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 175 — Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 437. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having had Darshan at Thirupparaythurai, continued his Thalam pilgrimage. Sekkizhar Peruman sings as follows: “Having worshipped other Thiru-Pathis and performed sacred services, he praised with Thiru-Pathigams. With abundant grace, he crossed the Kaveri, and reaching the northern bank, he arrived at Thiruppaingili, where the archers reside.” Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman describes the pilgrimage undertaken by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Having worshipped Thirupparaythurai and other Thiru-Pathis nearby, he then crossed the Kaveri to the northern bank and reached the Thalam called Thiruppaingili, as sung by Sekkizhar Peruman.

Thirupparaythurai to Ari. He visited other Thiru-Pathis located nearby. These other Thiru-Pathis include Thiru-Alanthurai, Thiruchendurai, and similar places on the southern bank of the Kaveri.

However, Sivakavimani Ayyavargal notes that the Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar for these places are not available. In the Dharumaiyatheena Periya Purana Vilakkam, it is noted that the nearby Thiru-Pathis mentioned in this verse are Thiru-Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vatpokki. This is because one Thiru-Pathigam each, sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, has been found for Thiru-Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vatpokki.

Therefore, it is believed that he must have visited the Thalam of Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vatpokki, which are south of the Kaveri from Thirupparaythurai, and then crossed the Kaveri to the northern bank to reach Thiruppaingili. This note is found in the Dharumaiyatheena Periya Purana Vilakkam.

Accordingly, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrives at the sacred Thalam called Thiru-Kadambanthurai.

Here, we have received a Thiru-Pathigam sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in praise of the Lord. This Thalam, known as Thiru-Kadambanthurai, is currently called Kadambar Kovil and Kulithalai.

Here, the sacred name of the Lord is Kadambavaneswarar, Kadambavanathar. The sacred name of the Goddess is Balakujambal. The Theertham is the Kaveri. Those who worshipped the Lord here include Brahma, Vishnu, the Saptha Kanniyars, and others. The unique feature of this Thalam is that the temple is oriented towards the north, and the Lord also faces north. This is the only Thalam among the Thevara-sung Sthalams that faces north, which is a unique feature of this Thalam.

This is a unique feature of this Thalam. There are 274 Thevara-sung Sthalams, of which 127 are on the southern bank of the Kaveri. Among these, Thiru-Kadambanthurai is the second Thalam. Currently, everyone knows Kulithalai. This temple is located in the city of Kulithalai. Thiru-Kadambanthurai is one of the Thalam names ending with ‘thurai’.

It is currently known as Kadambar Kovil. Near Thiru-Kadambanthurai, on the southern bank of the Kaveri, are temples such as Rajendram, Pettaivaythalai, Vatpokki, Karuppathur, and on the northern bank are Thiru-Ingoy Malai, Musiri, Vellur, and other sacred places. On Thai Poosam day, the deities of these temples come to the Kaveri River and grant Darshan. It is customary to visit Kadambar Kovil in the morning, Vatpokki Malai in the afternoon, and Thiru-Ingoy Malai in the evening to receive great merit. It is customary to visit Thiru-Ingoy Malai in the evening and have Darshan of the deities there, which is considered highly meritorious. This is explained by the proverb: “Morning Kadambar, Afternoon Sokkar, Evening Thiru-Vengainathar.” To the east of Kadambar Kovil, outside the town of Kulithalai, is the Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple, which is a sub-temple of Kadambar Kovil.

This is the Thalam where Lord Shiva appeared in his wedding attire to the Brahmin named Vedasarma. Other temples include the Perallamman Temple, Mariamman Temple, Neelamega Perumal Temple, and others. This sacred Thalam has other sacred names besides Thiru-Kadambanthurai, such as Kadambai, Kadambavanam, Dakshina Kasi, Kulithanthalai, Brahmapuram, Chathurvedapuri, Kanthapuram, Sapthapuri, Vadmadurai, Gnanodayapuri, and others. These names exist. It is called Kadambanthurai, Kadambai, Kadambavanam because it had Kadambu trees. It is called Dakshina Kasi because it is located on the southern bank of the Kaveri, facing north, like Varanasi in the north.

It is called Kulithanthalai because it has cool groves. It is called Brahmapuram because Brahma worshipped here, built temples, and conducted chariot festivals. It is called Chathurvedapuri because Vishnu recovered the Vedas from Somakasura here. It is called Kanthapuram because Muruga worshipped here to remove his curse and received blessings. It is called Gnanodayapuri because Muruga attained enlightenment here. It is called Sapthapuri because the Saptha Kanniyars worshipped the Lord here and were freed from the Brahmahathi Dosha that afflicted them.

It is called Vadmadurai because the Brahmin Vedasarma performed penance here and witnessed the wedding scene that took place in Madurai. And so, this Thalam is known by these sacred names. The Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple in this town is the place where Lord Shiva appeared in his wedding attire to the Brahmin named Vedasarma. The name Kulithanthalai has evolved into Kulithalai and is now commonly used.

Here, as a symbol of the Saptha Kanniyars’ worship of the Lord, their idols are placed behind the Moolavar in the temple. The temple is situated amidst lush green groves, facing north. Among the north-facing temples, Varanasi in the north and Kadambar Kovil in the south are particularly significant. This is why this Thalam is called Dakshina Kasi. The Lord, Muruga, and the Goddess are all seated together, making the temple appear like a Somaskanda Murthy. The Kaveri River flows to the north.

Inside the temple, there are two circumambulatory paths, and outside, there is a street for the chariot procession. In front of the temple, there is a mandapam and an entrance. Inside, in the second circumambulatory path, to the east, there are a vehicle mandapam, a kitchen, a well, and a shrine for Kalabhairavar. In the southeast corner, there is the Brahma Theertham. In the northwest corner, there is the Navaratri Mandapam. Next to it, the Amman temple faces east.

Opposite, there are flagstaffs for the Lord and Amman, and a shrine for Paramnathar.

Following this, the inner gopuram entrance has three eyes. Passing through this, inside the first circumambulatory path, there are shrines for Natarajar, Navagrahas, and Chandikeswarar. To the south, there are shrines for Jeshtadevi, Nallvar, Arupathu Moovar, and Sekkizhar Peruman. To the west, there are shrines for Viswanathar, Vinayagar, Subramaniyar, Somaskandar, and Gajalakshmi. In the center, there is the Maha Mandapam and the Moolavar Garbhagriham. In the Moolasthanam, Kadambainathar is seated in the form of a Lingam.

Behind the Moolavar. There are idols of the Saptha Kanniyars. Outside the temple, there is the Sri Balakujambal Kalyana Mandapam. The sacred tree of the Thalam, the Kadamba tree, is inside the temple.

The Lord residing in this Thalam is named Kadambavanathar because he is in Kadambavanam. He is also known by the names Sundaresar and Soundaresar. Since Brahma worshipped him, he is also called Brahmesar. The Goddess is named Balakujambal. In Tamil, the Goddess is called Muttrila Mulaiyammai. The name Thiruveni is also mentioned.

Vinayagar is revered as Siddhi Vinayagar. Paramnathar is the guardian deity. The names of the deities from other village temples that come to the Kaveri on Thai Poosam day in this Thalam are as follows: on the southern bank of the Kaveri. The temples and the sacred names of the Lord and Goddess are: Rajendram: Lord’s name is Mathyārjunēśvarar, Goddess’s name is Dēvanāyaki. Pettaivāythalai: Mathyārjunēśvarar, Dēvanāyaki. Thiruvāṭpōkki: Lord’s name is Ratnagirīśvarar, Goddess’s name is Surumbārkuḻali.

Karuppattūr: Lord’s sacred name is Simmapurīśvarar, Goddess’s sacred name is Sugandakuntalāmbāḷ.

Now, the temples on the northern bank of the Kaveri: Thiru-Īṅkōymalai: Lord’s name is Maragathāccalēśvarar, Goddess is Maragathāmbāḷ. Muśiri: Lord’s sacred name is Candramauḷīśvarar, Goddess is Karpūravalli. Veḷḷūr: Lord’s sacred name is Thirukāmīśvarar, Goddess’s sacred name is Sivakāmiyammai.

Now, the Theerthams of this Thalam: The Kaveri River flows to the north of the temple. On Thai Poosam day, Kadambavanathar and the deities from other village temples come and grant Darshan. It is believed that the rivers Ganga, Yamuna, Saraswati, and others merged with the Kaveri River in the month of Aippasi and benefited from it.

Next, the Brahma Theertham is located in the Agni corner of the second circumambulatory path inside the temple. It serves as a symbol of Brahma’s worship. In addition to this, there are many other Theerthams. This sacred Thalam is special due to its Murthy, Thalam, and Theertham. The Dasangams (ten attributes) of Kadambavanathar are described in the book ‘Kadambavanathar Ula’. The mountain associated with the Lord is Kailasa Malai, the river is Kaveri Nadi, the country is Chola Nadu, the city is Kadambar Kovil, the garland is Konrai Malai, the horse is the horse of the Vedas, the elephant is Airavanam, the flag is Rishaba Kodi, the drum is Pranavam, and the command is the command that keeps the sun, moon, and other entities in their proper places without deviation.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Arunagirinathar, Aiyadigal Kadavar Kon, and others worshipped the Lord of this Thalam. And accordingly, sang devotional hymns such as Thevaram and Thiruppugazh. According to puranic history, this is the Thalam where Lord Shiva appeared to Kanva Muni and the Devas under a Kadamba tree. Among the Utsava Murthies, there are two Nataraja Murthies and two Somaskanda Murthies. During the renovation of the temple, one Nataraja Utsava Murthy without Muyalagan and one Somaskanda Murthy were found buried in the second circumambulatory path. They are now displayed in their respective shrines.

In the month of Aani, a festival is held where the Nataraja Murthy without Muyalagan and the Nataraja Murthy with Muyalagan on Margazhi Thiruvathirai day come out and grant Darshan. The idol of the Goddess is also a beautiful and compassionate form. Daily pujas are performed in this temple, including Thiru-Ananthal Puja in the early morning, morning puja, Uchikala Puja, Sayarakshai, and Ardha Jama Puja. Daily pujas are performed. Annually, in the month of Maasi, the grand festival of Brahmotsavam begins on the Aswathi star and lasts for ten days. Daily, the deities are taken out in procession on various vehicles.

On the fifth day, the Rishaba Vahana Darshan takes place, on the ninth day, the Thiru Therottam (chariot procession), and on the tenth day, the Theerthavari (sacred bath). It is stated in the Sthala Puranam that this festival was initiated by Brahma in the month of Chithirai and concluded with Theerthavari on the Chithirai star.

Now, the Thai Poosam festival is one of the main festivals celebrated in this Thalam. On the Poosam star in the month of Thai, Kadambanthurainathar and the Goddess, seated on a Rishaba Vahanam, proceed to the Kaveri riverbank in a beautiful palanquin, perform Theertham, and then sit in the decorated pandal specially erected for the Poosam festival to grant Darshan. As we have already seen, other deities from nearby temples will also arrive. Other deities from nearby temples will also arrive and grant Darshan simultaneously. At night, pujas and aradhanas will be performed for all the deities at the same time. When the above-mentioned eight temple deities arrive and depart, a meeting deeparadhanai will be performed.

On Poosam day, all the deities will stay in the pandal throughout the night. The next morning, all the deities will depart and return to their respective sacred places. In the month of Panguni, on Uthiram day, the Asthira Devar will go to the Kaveri and perform Theertham. At night, the Lord and Goddess will be taken out in procession on a Rishaba Vahanam. On Chithirai New Year’s Day and Full Moon Day, the Lord and Goddess will be taken out in procession on a Rishaba Vahanam at night. On Vaikasi Visakam day, Subramaniyar, Valli, and Deivayanai will be taken out in procession on a peacock Vahanam.

On Aani Uthiram day, Abhishekam will be performed for Natarajar, and the Natarajar without Muyalagan will be taken out in procession. In the month of Aadi. In the month of Aadi, the Aadi Pooram festival for the Goddess will be celebrated for ten days. On Pooram day, only the Goddess’s chariot will be drawn. In Aavani, the Aavani Moola festival will take place for two days, featuring the rope-changing ceremony and the mud-carrying festival for Puttu. In Purattasi, the Navaratri festival will be celebrated for ten days, with the Goddess seated in Kolu and a procession on Vijayadasami day.

At the beginning of Aippasi, the Panchamurthy procession will take place, where the deities perform Theertham in Thula Kaveri. In the morning, they will go to the Kaveri and return, and at night, the Panchamurthies will go on a street procession in a silver Rishabam. In the Skanda Sashti festival, the Soorasamharam will take place on the sixth day, and the wedding of Valli and Deivayanai on the seventh day. On the full moon day, Annabhishekam will be performed. In the month of Karthigai, on Karthigai day, a Deepa Darshan will be held with the burning of Sokkappanai. At night, the Panchamurthies will grant Darshan on a Rishaba Vahanam.

In Margazhi, Dhanur Masa Puja will be performed in the early morning. The Thiruvathirai festival will last for ten days. The Thiruvathirai festival takes place. On Thiruvathirai day, Natarajar Darshan occurs. The Natarajar with Muyalagan comes out and grants Darshan. In the early morning, Thiruvambavai and Thiruppalli Ezhuchi songs are recited.

On the first day of the month of Thai, the Lord and Goddess will appear on a silver Rishabam and grant Darshan. On Mattu Pongal day, the Lord will be taken out in procession on a horse Vahanam. On Thai Poosam day, Kadambavanesar, along with other temple deities, will proceed to the Kaveri River, stay overnight, and return the next morning. The Poosam day festival will be celebrated separately. According to the Periya Puranam verse, “Maaninil Piranthar Perum Payan Mathisoodum Annalar Adiyarthamai Amuthu Seivithal Kanninal Avar Nal Vizha Polivu Kandu Arthal,” one should witness and experience these festivals to receive the grace of the Lord. There is a Purana written in Tamil prose from Sanskrit, combining the three Thalam of Kadambanthurai, Rathnagiri, and Thiru-Ingoy Malai.

It contains many historical accounts from Naimisarukkam to Yathirai Sarukkam. In the Uttarabagam of Skanda Puranam, the greatness of Kadambavanam Thalam, as narrated by Suta Muni to Shaunaka and other Rishis in Naimisaranya, is presented as the history of this Thalam.

Once, Brahma, feeling weary and disgusted with his creative work, prayed to the Lord for supreme bliss.

Lord Shiva then blessed Brahma as follows: “O Brahma, south of the Vindhya mountain, there are three forms of Sat, Chit, and Ananda in the Chola country. On the southern side of the vast Kaveri, there is the Arathana Malai, which is the form of Sat. On the northern side of the vast Kaveri, there is the Maragatha Malai, which is the form of Chit. And on the southern bank of the Kaveri, there is Thiru-Kadambanthurai, which is the form of Ananda. These three Thalam are in the form of Sachidananda. The greatness of these three Thalam is celebrated as ‘Morning Kadambar, Afternoon Chakkar, Evening Thiru-Ingoy Malainathar.’ Among them, reach Thiru-Kadambanthurai, which is the form of Ananda, bathe in the Thiru-Kaveri, and worship with devotion, performing Abhishekam with mantras three times a day, and then perform penance with deep meditation.” Thus, Lord Shiva blessed Brahma.

Accordingly, when Brahma came here, to this blissful Thalam, he attained the state of ‘Iruvinai Oppu, Malaparibagam, Sakthi Nipatham’ and was filled with ecstatic bliss. Brahma bathed in the Ponni River and worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rituals.

The Lord appeared to Brahma and said, “In this Thalam, establish temples for us, Uma, Ganesa, Subramaniyar, and other attendants. Create a Theertham in your name in the Agni corner. Perform daily and occasional festivals, and then attain the ultimate liberation of Siddhanta Mukthi, which is merging with us.” Thus, the Lord blessed Brahma and then merged into the Lingam.

Now, the history of the Saptha Mathas’ worship: Formerly, an Asura named Dhoomralochanan fought against Goddess Durga. When the Goddess was weakened by the Asura’s arrows, the Saptha Kanniyars fought the Asura with great fury. The Asura, unable to withstand them, fled and hid in the ashram of Sage Kathyayana, who was performing penance facing the sun. The Saptha Mathas, who came searching for the demon, mistook the meditating sage for the demon’s illusion and killed him. As a result, they were afflicted with the Brahmahathi Dosha. To get rid of it, the Kanniyars came to Kadambavanam, and upon their arrival, the Brahmahathi Dosha left them.

Formerly, an Asura named Somakan stole all the Vedas and went to the netherworld. The three Thalam of Thiru-Kadambanthurai, which is the form of Ananda, on the southern bank of the Kaveri, are arranged in the form of Sachidananda. The greatness of these three Thalam is celebrated as ‘Morning Kadambar, Afternoon Chakkar, Evening Thiru-Ingoy Malainathar.’ Among them, reach Thiru-Kadambanthurai, which is the form of Ananda, bathe in the Thiru-Kaveri, and worship with devotion, performing Abhishekam with mantras three times a day, and then perform penance with deep meditation.“ Thus, Lord Shiva blessed Brahma.

Accordingly, when Brahma came here, to this blissful Thalam, he attained the state of ‘Iruvinai Oppu, Malaparibagam, Sakthi Nipatham’ and was filled with ecstatic bliss. Brahma bathed in the Ponni River and worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rituals.

The Lord appeared to Brahma and said, “In this Thalam, establish temples for us, Uma, Ganesa, Subramaniyar, and other attendants. Create a Theertham in your name in the Agni corner. Perform daily and occasional festivals, and then attain the ultimate liberation of Siddhanta Mukthi, which is merging with us.” Thus, the Lord blessed Brahma and then merged into the Lingam.

Now, the history of the Saptha Mathas’ worship: Formerly, an Asura named Dhoomralochanan fought against Goddess Durga. When the Goddess was weakened by the Asura’s arrows, the Saptha Kanniyars fought the Asura with great fury. The Asura, unable to withstand them, fled and hid in the ashram of Sage Kathyayana, who was performing penance facing the sun. The Saptha Mathas, who came searching for the demon, mistook the meditating sage for the demon’s illusion and killed him. As a result, they were afflicted with the Brahmahathi Dosha. To get rid of it, the Kanniyars came to Kadambavanam, and upon their arrival, the Brahmahathi Dosha left them.

Formerly, an Asura named Somakan stole all the Vedas and went to the netherworld. He went to the netherworld. Disturbed by this, Vishnu and other Devas reached Kadambavanam and performed great penance. As a result of their penance, Vishnu took the Matsya Avatar, went to the netherworld, killed the Asura, brought back the Vedas, and consecrated them in Kadambavanam.

Hence, this Thalam is called Vedapuri. A sinner named Devasarma, unable to bear his suffering, visited many sacred places to attain happiness and reached this Thalam.

Here, he donated a Kapila cow to Sage Agastya, who was worshipping the Lord and Goddess. With the Panchagavya of that cow, both of them performed Abhishekam and Aradhana to the Lord and Goddess, and they saw the Lord directly. Devasarma became Vedasarma. In response to his prayer, the Lord and Goddess granted the vision of the Meenakshi Sundareswarar wedding here. Formerly, when Lord Shiva was imparting the meaning of Pranava to Goddess Uma in Kailasa, Lord Muruga secretly listened without a Guru. For that reason, Lord Shiva cursed Lord Muruga to become dumb.

He went to the netherworld. Disturbed by this, Vishnu and other Devas reached Kadambavanam and performed great penance. As a result of their penance, Vishnu took the Matsya Avatar, went to the netherworld, killed the Asura, brought back the Vedas, and consecrated them in Kadambavanam.

Hence, this Thalam is called Vedapuri. A sinner named Devasarma, unable to bear his suffering, visited many sacred places to attain happiness and reached this Thalam.

Here, he donated a Kapila cow to Sage Agastya, who was worshipping the Lord and Goddess. With the Panchagavya of that cow, both of them performed Abhishekam and Aradhana to the Lord and Goddess, and they saw the Lord directly. Devasarma became Vedasarma. In response to his prayer, the Lord and Goddess granted the vision of the Meenakshi Sundareswarar wedding here. Formerly, when Lord Shiva was imparting the meaning of Pranava to Goddess Uma in Kailasa, Lord Muruga secretly listened without a Guru. For that reason, Lord Shiva cursed Lord Muruga to become dumb.

Lord Shiva cursed Lord Muruga to become dumb. To be freed from this curse, Lord Muruga visited many Shiva Sthalams and worshipped Lord Shiva. He then reached Thiru-Kadambanthurai, bathed in the Thiru-Kaveri, performed Abhishekam and worshipped Muttrilamu Ammai and Kadambavanathar, and was freed from his dumbness. He then praised and worshipped the Lord with many Vedas.

Therefore, this Thalam is named Kanthapuram. Goddess Uma took Kumara Kadavul, embraced him, kissed his forehead, and made him sit beside Umanathar.

Therefore, those who lovingly worship the Somaskanda Murthy residing here will easily attain Gnana and Mukthi. There is also a note on how to perform the pilgrimage. One should bathe in the Kaveri in the early morning, perform daily rituals, take fragrant flowers, go to the Kadambavaneswarar temple, and have Darshan of the Lord, Goddess, and other deities.

There, one should make a Sankalpam for the pilgrimage and then. After performing good deeds, one should go to the Kaveri River, fill a pot with water, meditate facing the Ayyarmalai, also known as Vaatpokki, then ascend Ayyarmalai.

There, one should worship Thiru-Rathnagireeswarar, who is enshrined facing west, and Ambigai Aralakesi, performing Abhishekam and Aradhanai with the Kaveri water brought from Kadambavanam. From there, one should cross the Kaveri and reach Thiru-Eengoymalai, also known as Maragathachalam, ascend the mountain, worship the Lord and Ambigai, and then return to Kadambanthurai for worship. One should stay there that night, and the next morning, bathe in the Kaveri, perform charities, visit the temple, and complete the pilgrimage. Doing so is equivalent to performing a Ganga pilgrimage a hundred times and a Sethu pilgrimage a thousand times. Those who read and listen to this Purana will attain all siddhis.

Thus, we too have become sanctified, said Suta Mahamuni to the Naimisaranya Munis. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, who arrived at the Thiru-Sthalam from Thiru-Parayathurai, composed a Thiru-Pathigam. Worshipping the Lord here, this Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam is the eighteenth Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thiru-Murai. This Thiru-Pathigam begins with the Mother’s sacred name, “Mutrilaa Mulaiyaal.” Mutrilaa Mulaiyaal Ivalaagilum, Attranthirkkum Arivilaagilum, Kattrach Chenchadaiyaan Kadambanthurai, Petra Moorthi Endraal Engal Pedhaiye. Thanagirunthathor Thanmaiyaraagilum, Unagu Theerthozhuthezhuminhalo, Kanagapun Chadaiyaan Kadambanthu, Ninaiyavallavar Neelvishumbaazhvare.

Aariyan Thamizhode Isaiyaanavan, Kooriyagunaathaar Kuri Nindravan, Kaarigaiyudaiyaan Kadambanthurai, Seeriyal Paththar Sendradai Minhale. Pannin Inmozhi Ketkum Paramanai, Vannanan Malan Pala Dhevarum Kannanum. Ariyaan Kadambanthurai Nanna Nam Vinaiyaayina Naasame. Marai Kondu Ammanaththaanai Manaththulai, Nirai Kondan Nenjinul Ura Vaimino, Karaikandan Uraiyum Kadambanthurai, Sirai Kondruvinai Theerath Thozhumine. Nangai Paagam Vaiththan Narunjothiyai, Pangamindri Paninthazhuminhalo, Gangai Senchadaiyaan Kadambanthurai, Angammoathi Aran Uraigindrathe. Ariya Naanmarai Aarangam Aam Ainthu, Puriyan Dhevarhal Eththa Nanjundavan, Kariya Kandaththinaan Kadambanthurai, Uriya Vaaru Ninai Mada Nenjame.

Poomenn Kothai Umaior Paaganai, Oomanjeythum Unarminhal Ullaththaal, Kaamarkkaaynthapiraan Kadambanthurai, Naamam Eththa Nam Theevinai Naasame. Paaranangi Vanangi Pani Seyya, Naaranan Piraman Ariyaathathor, Kaaranan Kadambanthurai Meviya Aa. Aranangu Oru Paal Udai Mainthane, Noolaal Nandraa Ninaiminhal Noikada, Paal Aanainthudan Aadum Paramanar, Kaalaal Oondrugandhaan Kadambanthurai, Melaanaan Seytha Valvinai Veedume.

Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped Thiru-Kadambanthurai, proceeds to Thiru-Vaatpokki Thiru-Sthalam.

We shall go on reflecting.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 176 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 438, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having worshipped Thiru-Kadambanthurai, reaches the Thiru-Sthalam named Thiru-Vaatpokki. Other sacred names for this place are Ayyarmalai, Rathnagiri, and Sivayamalai. The sacred name of the Lord here is Rathnagireesar, Arathanaachaleswarar, Manikka Eesar, Mudithazhumbar. The sacred name of the Goddess is Surumbaarkuzhali, Aralakesi.

The Sthala Viruksham (sacred tree) is the Neem tree. The Theertham (sacred water body) is the Kaveri River. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman has sung about this Sthalam as a Vaippu Sthalam in the ninth Thiru-Pathigam of the second Thiru-Murai. Appar Swamigal has composed a Thiru-Pathigam here. This Sthalam is currently popularly known as Ayyarmalai. The legend states that an Aryan king, who came seeking a ruby, was shown a pit by the Lord and asked to fill it with Kaveri water.

When it did not fill, the king, angered, raised his sword, and the Lord bestowed a ruby upon him. The king, whose mind was transformed, did not desire the ruby but attained liberation by performing service to Shiva. It is said that the king’s act of cutting gave the Lord the sacred name Mudithazhumbar, and the scar from the cut can be seen on the upper part of the Shiva Lingam. It is believed that crows do not frequent this mountain because a crow that overturned the milk an herdsman was carrying for the Lord was incinerated.

Hence, this place is also called Kaagam Anugaamalai (the mountain where crows do not approach). The phrase “Kaagam Mepooril Kadunthidum Parambu” is from the Thiru-Nagaikkaaron Puranam. The Purana of this Sthalam is narrated as having been revealed by Suta Mahamuni to other sages in Naimisaranya. This Sthalam is one of the places where the peaks of Mount Meru fell during the battle between Adisesha and Vayu. By merely seeing Rathnagireeswarar, all sins are removed. The force with which this mountain fell to the earth, one part of it is submerged underground.

It is sixteen yojanas high and three yojanas wide. There are sacred waters, including the highly potent Deva Theertham. The Rathna Lingam was worshipped by Uma Devi. There are eight Theerthams here. The Deva Theertham is at the summit of the mountain. Many sages are performing severe penance here.

This mountain is the form of Panchakshara itself, where the Lord, who is the essence of the Vedas, is seated. To atone for the sin of desiring Ahalya, Indra, on the advice of Brihaspati, came to Rathnachalam and installed a neem tree in front of the Goddess’s shrine. At the summit of the mountain, he created a Theertham with his Vajrayudha, and daily in the morning, he would chant the Thrayambaka Mantra, bathe in that Theertham, and worship the Lord and Ambigai with fragrant flowers brought from Devaloka.

Thus, his sin was removed. Indra’s worship, pleased the Peruman, who appeared with Ambigai on a Rishabha Vahanam to Indra.

At that time, Indra praised the Lord. Those who recite that hymn at the end of Shiva Puja will attain the eight kinds of wealth. During auspicious times such as Dakshinayana, Uttarayana, Vishu, solar and lunar eclipses, Amavasya, Somavaram, Janma Nakshatram, and Shraddha Dinam, if one bathes in Deva Theertham, chanting the Ayahi Mantra three times, performs Abhishekam to the neem tree, worships the Lord and Ambigai, and then performs Kanyadanam, one will attain Shivlokam. A king who donates houses and agricultural lands to Brahmins within five krosas around Rathnachalam will attain the form of Shiva. If one stays here for a month, bathes in Deva Theertham, and worships the neem tree, severe diseases like leprosy, paralysis, and tumors will be cured. If one consumes the naturally fallen neem leaves, the blind will regain sight, the deaf will regain hearing, the mute will regain speech, those with speech impediments will speak well and receive good education, those with physical deformities will attain beautiful bodies, and those without children will be blessed with progeny.

Those who recite the glory of the neem tree in the presence of Shiva will attain the boon of liberation. Formerly, to atone for the sin of uprooting the peaks of Mount Meru with his might, Vayu Deva came to Rathnagiri, established a Theertham in his name, and daily performed Archana to the Lord Rathnagireeswarar with flowers and leaves. On a Purnima day in the month of Thula, at the end of the puja, the Peruman, pleased with his devotion, appeared with Uma Devi and blessed Vayu Deva to pervade the entire world and exist in every body with ten names: Prana, Apana, Vyana, Udana, Samana, Naga, Kurma, Krukara, Devadatta, and Dhananjaya. Vayu Deva, having learned the history of being freed from his curse through Narada Muni, Adisesha also came to this earthly realm to atone for the sin of having participated in shaking Meru. He visited the Sthalams of Gokarnam, Sangakarnam, Prabhasam, Anandasailam, Someswaram, Kapileswaram, Sahiyamalai in Kerala, Srikandam, Vilvaranyam, Dharmeswaram, Vyasashramam, Suchindram, Avinashi, Bhavanikkoodal, Varahakkoodal, Swethachalam, Karuvur, Valeeswaram, Agastheeswaram, Thiru-Vaiyaaru, Arapazheeswaram, Analeeswaram, Neengoymalai, Kadambavanam, and Sankarachalam.

Then he reached Rathnagiri, worshipped the sages Vyasarathri, Bharadwajar, Jamadagni, Kathyayanar, Adisringar, and Mayuramukhar who were performing penance there. He installed a Kungiliyam tree, created a pond near it in his name, invoked the Nidhi Sanghanidhi and others in the middle of the Theertham, and chanted the Panchakshara Mantra one thousand and eight times. He then brought one hundred and eight pots of water from the Gangachala Theertham established by Surya, performed Abhishekam to the Peruman, and worshipped Him. The Lord, pleased with Adisesha’s worship, appeared before him and graciously removed his sin, so it is said.

Furthermore, Suta Muni states that Shiva’s transgression can only be removed at this Sthalam. Among the mantras, like Gayatri, Rathnagiri is the best among the five peaks of Meru. Sins committed elsewhere will be removed if one comes here, but sins committed here will only be removed here. Those who establish a Nandavanam (flower garden) or light lamps here will attain the form of Shiva. Merely contemplating this Sthalam can lead to liberation. Bathing in Naga Theertham on Purattasi Suklapaksha Chaturdashi can remove Shiva’s offense.

Bathing in Surya Pushkarani during a solar eclipse can cure diseases like leprosy and epilepsy. Performing Thilatharpanam here for a long time, one can live in Kailasa, said Suta Muni. On an island called Mandhegam near Udayachalam, powerful rakshasas, who had gained strength through penance, would battle with Surya at dawn. Surya was unable to defeat them. According to an ethereal voice, Surya sent Asani here to worship at Rathnachalam. Asani created a Theertham in Surya’s name and performed pujas to the Lord.

The pleased Lord then granted Surya the power to defeat those rakshasas. Narada requested Agastya Muni, who was performing penance on the banks of the Pushpabhadra River north of the Himalayas, to accompany him on a pilgrimage. Both set out and visited Kashmir, Prabhasam, Vilvaranyam, Ketharam, Kashi, Prayagai, Avanti, and Gomati.

Then, to visit Kusala Kshethram, Narada took leave of Agastya and departed. Agastya then visited Shiva Kshethrams and, in the Vindhya Mountains, saw a corpse, learned its history, and, out of compassion, desired to grant it a good afterlife. With that corpse, Agastya Muni reached Kadambavanam.

There, as soon as he sprinkled Kaveri water on it, the corpse attained a divine body, worshipped the Muni, praised Kadambavananathar and Ambigai, ascended a Vimanam, and reached Kailasa. Agastya continuously worshipped Shiva, who is enshrined facing north in Kadambavanam, from sunset. The next morning, at sunrise, the Peruman appeared before him to bestow grace.

Then, Agastya reached Rathnagiri, created a Theertham in his name on the western side, and invoked all Theerthams, including Ganga, into it. He himself bathed in it and, at noon, performed Abhishekam to the Peruman and worshipped Him.

At that time, the Lord appeared to Agastya. Agastya prayed, “Please initiate me into the Sri Panchakshara Maha Mantra.” The Peruman, adorned with all ornaments, appeared as Sundarar with Aralakesi Ambigai, placed His sacred hands on Agastya’s head, and initiated him into the Panchakshara Mantra. Agastya attained Jeevan Mukti. Agastya prayed to the Lord, “Since you have appeared to me at noon, you should be known by the sacred name Madhyana Sundarar. From today onwards, those who have darshan during the day should attain liberation.” The Lord granted his wish. This Sthalam is where the Peruman blessed a king named Veerasenan.

The Theertham created by Bharadwaja Muni through penance and the Theertham created by Vishnu in the form of a boar in the Agni direction are present here. To the north of this mountain is the Kanya Theertham created by Durga Devi.

There, she was freed from the sin of slaying Mahisha. Bathing in the Mahanadi there grants all siddhis. Since Durga Devi took Mahisha’s life with the sword granted by Shiva, it is said that the name Vaat- Naatpokki came into being. A herdsman from Kanchi, seeking progeny for his sister, came to this Sthalam and, upon his prayer being fulfilled, offered his head as a sacrifice. Due to his detachment, he is known as Vairaperumal. His shrine and a neem tree are located on the way to the mountain.

After the Deeparadhanai for Rathnagireeswarar, Deeparadhanai is performed for him, the guardian deity of the mountain. A herdsman from Kulithalai used to bring a pot of fresh milk daily for Abhishekam.

One day, a crow overturned the pot of milk, and the herdsman, grieved, decided to end his life. At that moment, the Lord appeared and said, “My devotee, do not grieve. This mountain is my form. The milk spilled on it is like an Abhishekam to me.” He then incinerated the crow.

Since then, crows do not fly here. The Sthala Purana states that the Lord appeared to Sundaramurthy Swamigal here as a Jyotirlingam and the entire mountain as rubies, and bestowed gold on a rock. That rock is called Pon Idum Paarai (the rock that gives gold). This event is part of the Chithirai Brahmotsavam on the fifth day. Since Durga’s curse was removed, two rock fissures, a sword-like rock nearby, and the Sapta Kannikas can be seen on the mountain. The legend says that when the seven maidens were struggling without shelter during heavy rain, the Lord created a cave-like structure between the rocks here and gave them refuge.

The people of Poompuhar, having left their city, settled here and, amazed, offered their twelfth share to the Lord.

Therefore, the Lord here is called Panirendam Chettiyar (the twelfth merchant). On Shivaratri or the days before or after, sunlight passes through a window directly facing the Lord and falls upon the Lord. In front of the Shiva Lingam, there is a water tank called Poyvasik Kopparai.

Here, ten pots of water are brought daily from the nearby Kaveri for the Lord’s noon Abhishekam. Even today, the descendants of the Panirendam Chettiyar family undertake this responsibility and conduct it through the temple priests. Since a king worshipped here, the Lord is known by the sacred name Rajalingamoorthy. It is believed that if snakes bite on this mountain, the venom will not spread. During dry seasons, if Abhishekam is performed for Sagunakundru Vinayagar, it rains. The milk offered as Abhishekam to the Shiva Lingam turns into curd within a few moments.

Every full moon, devotees circumambulate this herb-rich mountain. While circumambulating, if one stands near the Kaattupillaiyar temple and loudly calls out “Manikka Malaiyane,” an echo is heard. These are all the glories of this Sthalam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having departed from Thiru-Kadambanthurai, arrives here. He worships the Lord of this Sthalam and composes a Thiru-Pathigam. It is the eighty-sixth Thiru-Pathigam, a Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam, in the fifth Thiru-Murai.

Kaala Paasam Pidithezhuth Thoothuvar, Baalagar Viruththar Pazhaiyaarenaar, Aala Neerhal Amarntha Vaatpokkiyar, Seelamaarnthavar Semmaiyul Nirpare. Viduththa Thoothuvar Vanthu Vinaikkuzhi, Paduththapothu Payanilai Paavikaal, Aduththa Kinnarang Ketkum Vaatpokkiyay, Eduththum Eththiyum Inburuminhale. Vanthivaaru Valaiththazhuth Thoothuvar, Unthiyodi Narahaththidaamunam, Anthiyin Oli Thaangum Vaatpokkiyar, Sinthiyaa Ezhvaar Vinai Theerpare. Kootram Vanthu Kumaiththidum Pothinaar, Thetram Vanthu Thelivu Uralaagume. Aatravum Arul Seyyum Vaatpokki Paal, Ettrumin Vilakkai Irul Neengave.

Maarukondu Valaiththazhuth Thoothuvar, Veru Veru Paduppathan Munname, Aaru Senchadai Vaiththa Vaatpokkiyaarkku, Oori Oori Urugum En Ullame. Kaanamodi Kadithazhuth Thoothuvar, Thaanamodu Thalaipidiyamunam, Aananjadiyugandha Vaatpokkiyar, Oonamillavarkku Unmaiyil Nirpare. Paarththu Paasam Pidithezhuth Thoothuvar, Koorththa Velaar Kumaipathan Munname, Aarththa Gangai Adakkum Vaatpokkiyar, Keerththimaigal Kilarndhuraiminhale. Naadivanthu Naman Thamar Nal Irul, Koodivanthu Kumaipathan Munname, Aadal Paadal Ugandha Vaatpokkiyay, Vaadi Eththa Nam Vaattam Thavirame. Kattaruththuk Kadithazhuth Thoothuva, Pottu Nokkip Purappadaame, Attamaama, Malar Soodum Vaatpokkiyaarkku, Ittamaagi Inaiyadi Eththume. Irakkam Munnariyaathu Ezhuthoothuvar, Parakkaliththavar Pattruthan Munname, Arakkanukkarul Seytha Vaatpokkiyar, Karappathum Karappar Avar Thangatkke.

We shall continue to reflect on the Purana of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 177 — Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 439, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having departed from Thiru-Parayathurai, crosses the Kaveri River and ascends its northern bank, after visiting Sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri such as Thiru-Alandurai, Thiru-Chendurai, and also Thiru-Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vaatpokki. Appar Swamigal reaches the Thiru-Sthalam named Thiru-Paingili.

At this time, the gracious event of the Lord providing Appar Swamigal with a packed meal (Kattuchoru, Potichoru) is about to occur. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having crossed the Kaveri and ascended its northern bank, continues his journey towards the Thiru-Sthalam named Thiru-Paingili. As he travels towards Thiru-Paingili, his body becomes extremely exhausted and weary. He becomes thirsty, and along with it, hunger also sets in. These feelings of hunger and thirst are emotions that can make all our physical and mental efforts falter.

However, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is in the state of a Jeevan Mukta.

Therefore, neither this hunger nor thirst disturbed his mind or consciousness in the slightest.

Thus, even with hunger and thirst, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman continues to proceed, determined to reach Thiru-Paingili. Nevertheless, Lord Shiva decides to alleviate Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s hunger and thirst. Brahma Deva, who is difficult to perceive even when flying in the form of a swan in the sky, and Vishnu, who is difficult to perceive even when digging into the earth in the form of a boar, Lord Shiva Himself comes there to be seen by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. He comes on the very road leading to Thiru-Paingili. How does He come? He creates a cool grove along the path.

He creates a beautiful pond filled with water. The water filled in the pond is created by the Peruman to quench thirst and alleviate water-longing. He creates the grove to relieve the weariness of the journey. He comes ahead on the road leading to Thiru-Paingili, anticipating when His devotee, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, will arrive. Even now, Shiva Peruman is seated there in such a manner, before the time of his arrival. He is seated thus on the path he will take.

How is he seated? As a Brahmin adorned with sacred ash. Sacred ash is that which perpetually adheres to the hearts and sacred forms of devotees. Shiva Peruman, as a Brahmin adorned with such sacred ash, created a pond and a grove on the road leading to Thiru-Paingili, and awaits the arrival of his devotee, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Even though Thirunavukkarasu Peruman might experience thirst, hunger, and weariness, the groves and ponds here would not captivate his mind, nor could they.

But Peruman is seated as a Brahmin adorned with sacred ash, and that sacred ash ...will indeed captivate the mind of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, to enchant his devotee and bring him under his sway, the Lord awaits there as a Brahmin smeared with sacred ash.

Furthermore, having created groves and ponds and seated himself as a Brahmin adorned with sacred ash, the Lord also awaits with a bundle of cooked rice (pothichoru) to alleviate Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s hunger. Pothichoru refers to rice packed and tied, also known as kattuchoru (packed meal). It is called pothichoru because it contains rice along with its accompanying curries and other provisions.

Thus, with this pothichoru, to quench Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s hunger, and having created a pond to slake his thirst, and a grove to relieve his weariness ...Peruman is seated as a Brahmin adorned with sacred ash on the path of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having arrived at this spot on the way to Thiru-Paingili, sees the Brahmin adorned with sacred ash and approaches him. The Lord, who has the bull as his vehicle, seated there in the guise of a Brahmin adorned with sacred ash, beholds Thirunavukkarasu Peruman who has arrived, and graciously says, “You are very weary from walking a long distance. Eat this packed meal I have, drink the water from this pond, and relieve your fatigue.” This divine intention of Shiva Peruman, seated there, towards Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, is a gracious intent aimed at bringing his devotee under his control. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “You have come a long way and are weary; eat this packed meal from me, drink water from this overflowing pond, relieve your fatigue, and then depart.” Peruman requests him to eat the packed meal he has. The rice here also signifies the ultimate truth of liberation.

“Pathagame soru pattrinava tholnokkam” is from Thiruvachagam. As the Brahmin adorned with sacred ash spoke thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman accepts it as the Lord’s divine grace.

Moreover, the Brahmin spoke with great affection, as if already well-acquainted with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, urging him to eat.

Therefore, this is the Lord’s divine grace ...thinking thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, without further thought, accepted the packed meal, partook of the sweet food, drank the water, cleansed himself, and relieved his weariness. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman perceives everything as the result of divine grace.

Therefore, he accepted and ate the packed meal given by the Brahmin without refusal, considering it also as the Lord’s divine grace. Having eaten and relieved his fatigue, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was asked by the Brahmin present there, “Where are you going?” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman replied, “I am going to Thiru-Paingili.” Then, the incomparable Lord, that Brahmin, also said, “I too am going to that place.” Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, having eaten the packed meal and drunk water to relieve his fatigue on the way to Thiru-Paingili, did not think of resting there for a while longer but immediately attempted to proceed towards Thiru-Paingili.

Therefore, the Brahmin there also accompanied Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, saying, “I too am going to Thiru-Paingili.” Sekkizhar Peruman sings here, “When he, who is difficult to describe, said he was going to Thiru-Paingili, the incomparable one said, ‘I am going there,’ and went with him.” Sekkizhar Peruman uses the word ‘udan’ (with) here, indicating that Shiva Peruman, who came as a Brahmin, went along. This word ‘udan’ is unique to Saiva Siddhanta. This word ‘udan’ ...is used by Saiva Siddhanta scholars to explain the three fundamental truths of Saiva Siddhanta. The Siddhantic implication here is that the Lord is eternally present as one with every soul.

Thus, the Brahmin also accompanies Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to Thiru-Paingili. The term ‘Maraiyavanar’ (the one who conceals) suggests that he is hidden within the form of the Brahmin. It also implies that he will soon disappear. This term ‘Maraiyavanar’ conveys that he is praised by the Vedas, and is generally manifest to those who recite the Vedas.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar and that Brahmin reach Thiru-Paingili. As they are about to reach Thiru-Paingili ...very close to it, Shiva Peruman, who had accompanied Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar until then in the guise of a Brahmin, suddenly disappeared. He concealed the form of the Brahmin he had shown until then and returned to his all-pervading state. As the one who had traveled with him suddenly disappeared, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, whose greatness shone through true penance, realized that the one who had come was Shiva Peruman himself. He understood that it was Shiva Peruman who had kept a packed meal on the way for him, created a pond and a grove to relieve his fatigue, waited for him, quenched his hunger, thirst, and weariness, and had accompanied him as a fellow traveler. Realizing this, he praised Peruman, fell down, rose, and shed tears ...raining down, and melting, he immersed himself in divine bliss, exclaiming, “What immense grace is this that the Lord of Dance has bestowed upon me, even me, a humble servant!” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sings, “Even me, a humble servant.” This ‘adiyen’ (humble servant) implies “even me, who is good for nothing and wanders performing menial service.” With this sentiment, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman melts in devotion.

Now, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman composes a Thiru-Pathigam (sacred hymn) praising the Lord. He sings a Thiru-Pathigam with the theme, “The Lord of Dance bestowed grace upon me, making me worthy.” This Thiru-Pathigam was sung immediately after the Lord disappeared.

However, this Thiru-Pathigam is not currently available to us. Through the words of Sekkizhar Peruman, we learn that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sang this Thiru-Pathigam. This reference is available to us.

However, a Thiru-Pathigam sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman for the Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Paingili is currently available. It is the Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam titled ‘Udaiyarkovanam’. When was this sung? It was sung after Thirunavukkarasu Peruman went to the temple of Thiru-Paingili Thiru-Sthalam and had a darshan of the Lord. Even that hymn states: “When the Brahmin who came with him disappeared before him at Thiru-Paingili, the great one of true penance, realizing it was the Lord of Dance who had bestowed grace upon him, making him worthy, sang the song, fell, rose, and shed tears. He went to the temple of the Supreme Lord who resides in Paingili, worshipped the Lord with the dark throat, rejoiced greatly, and with true devotion and overflowing love, sang the Tamil garlands of hymns...”

...and performed extensive sacred service with love, remaining there,“ thus Sekkizhar Peruman composes the verses. When he arrived very close to the Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Paingili, the Lord who came as a Brahmin disappeared.

At that moment, he sang a hymn, and then, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar now enters the temple of Thiru-Paingili Thiru-Sthalam and has a darshan of Shiva Peruman enshrined there. He worships the Lord, Thiru-Neelakantar, enshrined there, rejoices greatly, and with true devotion and overflowing love, sings the Thevara Thiru-Pathigams, which are garlands of Tamil hymns, performs extensive sacred service, and remains there in Thiru-Paingili with love. The Thiru-Pathigam sung now is the Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam pertaining to the Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Paingili. Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam, Fifth Thirumurai, Forty-first Thiru-Pathigam.

“Udaiyarkovanam ondrum kuraivilar padaigal paridam soozhndha Paingiliyar sadaiyil gangai tharitha saduraraai adaiyavallavarkku illai avalame.” (Those who can reach the clever one who wears a loincloth, has no wants, is surrounded by hosts in Paingili, and holds Ganga in his matted locks, will have no sorrow.) “Mathamamalarsudiya mainthanar sitharaitthirivar vinai theerpparal patharthan thozhuthethu Paingili em athanai thozha vallavar nallare.” (The Lord who wears intoxicating flowers, wanders as a Siddha, removes karma; those who can worship our Father in Paingili, praised by devotees, are good.) “Vizhuthusoozhathan venmazhu vaazhpadai kazhuthu thunjirudkattagaththadalan pazhathonru inri Paingili paramanai thozhuthu selbavar tham vinai thoozhiye.” (The Lord who dances in
